speakeroldname: Mr. Egan Chambers (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: MR. CHAMBERS    CORRECTION OF NEWSPAPER AND RADIO REPORTS OF REMARKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to rise on a question of privilege and join the great body of the misquoted. Last night I was a member of a panel at a meeting of the "Voice of Women" here in Ottawa. This morning the Canadian Press issued a story from which I will quote briefly:
Canada needs Bomarc missiles equipped with nuclear warheads if Canada hopes to defend itself adequately, Egan Chambers .. . said here last night.
What I said was that Canada requires Bomarc missiles and quoted what has been said in this house, that these reach their maximum effectiveness with nuclear warheads. It will be recognized that this does not rule out the rejection of nuclear warheads for other reasons.
Also, this morning radio station CBO quoted me as follows:
Disarmament pronouncements of external affairs minister Howard Green have lost in general popularity because they are supported by certain radical elements.
What I did was urge the "Voice of Women" to give the maximum support to the practical and realistic disarmament efforts of the Secretary of State for External Affairs and say that I did not feel it was of assistance to him to advocate neutralism or unilateral disarmament.
This was an informal meeting and I had no text, but I have checked my recollection of what I said with other well known newspaper men who were present, and they substantiate my version. I should like to say that I appreciate the difficulty of writing an accurate and abbreviated press account of such a meeting, and I also appreciate the fact that the Canadian Press has issued a correction of its story.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DISCUSSIONS WITH U.K. PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Leader of the Opposition suggested that I might 90205-6-228J
give a short summary of what transpired during the visit to Ottawa of the right hon. Prime Minister of the United Kingdom. Though I do not feel free, as he realizes, to reveal the substance of the various private discussions which were held between Mr. Macmillan and myself during the visit, some general indication of the topics which were covered may be of interest.
One of the most important was the United Kingdom's relationship with Europe. This is a matter of major importance not only to the United Kingdom and the countries of Europe but to Canada itself, and indeed the whole western world. It should not be seen in purely economic terms, but as a broad development of much consequence in which there must be a careful weighing of both short and long term considerations and of political as well as economic factors. The United Kingdom government has these broad considerations in mind in examining the question of its relationship with Europe.
Reference has been made to the concept of an Atlantic community. As I indicated yesterday, these relationships among groupings in Europe and groupings in other regions of the world will take a very long time to develop and mature. It is well to recall, however, that to some extent the Atlantic community already exists, not in an institutional form but in a degree of spiritual fellowship and also in the various forms of co-operation in the military, political and economic spheres. It is naturally desirable, if not mandatory, in the interests of reinforcing the collective strength, stability and understanding of the western world, that co-operation should be expanded and intensified as practical possibilities permit.
I took the opportunity to restate the concern of the Canadian government regarding arrangements which the United Kingdom might work out with common market countries; that full account be taken of the trading interests of Canada. I made it clear that this would be particularly necessary in the field of agricultural products in which Canada has a substantial interest, and in respect of which the common market treaty has not yet led to specific trading arrangements. The Prime Minister of the United Kingdom left me with a clear impression that the United Kingdom government intends to make every effort to work out a satisfactory means of participating in the economic organization of Europe without detriment to Canadian or commonwealth

Discussions with U.K. Prime Minister interests. In this connection discussions will continue from time to time, and my hope is that, through continuing consultation, arrangements will be arrived at in keeping with Canada's wishes in this regard.
NATO is one subject which was discussed at some length, and the imperative need for greater efforts than have been made heretofore to bring NATO into a strong, flexible and understanding partnership was underlined. In addition, the need of moral, military and political capacity if NATO is to pursue its objectives successfully was emphasized.
The Leader of the Opposition, with his knowledge of the operation of NATO from its foundation, will realize that the importance of political consultation has been a subject of consideration throughout the years. Indeed, he belonged to the group known as the three wise men which made recommendations in this regard. I think Mr. Macmillan would agree that what requires development is the will and the readiness to consult well in advance. The machinery is there, and it cannot be blamed now for any shortcomings in consultation.
The question of a meeting of NATO heads of government was discussed. I feel such a meeting is necessary, but I am equally convinced that it should not be held until there has been thorough preparation and investigation in advance of the likely areas of agreement.
In the international field we reviewed the current situation in Laos and the Congo, but I do not think there is anything to report to the house, since the position in both these areas has been adequately reported in the press and in this chamber.
The problem of China is one to which attention was devoted. In particular, Mr. Macmillan and I discussed the question of Chinese representation in the United Nations and agreed that it was important to continue to work on this problem in preparation for the next regular session of the general assembly later this year.
The house is aware of the fact that the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom visited the West Indies before coming to the United States and Canada. During the course of our discussions he gave an account of the political situation in the West Indies and the outlook for the establishment of a federation when complete West Indies independence has been attained. The economic problems of the West Indies and the relationship of Canadian aid and other such programs to these problems in the western hemisphere were considered.
We discussed the question of low cost imports from Hong Kong, a matter of very
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
salient interest to Canadians at this time. As a result I believe a better understanding of the problems was arrived at, and further discussions will be continued by representatives of both governments.
Mention was made yesterday by the Leader of the Opposition to the uranium situation. On this matter both Mr. Macmillan and I had a word to say to the press following our meeting on Tuesday. Negotiations are continuing, and it would not be advantageous to go into this matter at this time. I might say that early meetings in London are anticipated to the end that negotiations will be resumed on the substance of this issue. In the meantime there is nothing to add to what I said in this regard when speaking in the house some week or ten days ago.
Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the
Opposition): Mr. Speaker, I think we can conclude from what the Prime Minister has said in his report to the house on the discussions between himself and the members of his government and the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom that perhaps the most important matter that came up was the United Kingdom making it quite clear-and indeed it was made quite clear by Mr. Macmillan in Washington-that the United Kingdom is moving toward a merger of the European free trade area and the common market. Indeed, as Mr. Macmillan is reported to have said in his press conference, that is the objective that the United Kingdom government has in mind. He was quoted as saying that once that merger has been achieved, and I quote from the press, "Then perhaps we can put together an Atlantic free trade area". These words confirm what Mr. Macmillan apparently said in Washington, and certainly what he said in a very important speech he made in Boston. He is reported as having said in that speech, and I quote from the Winnipeg Free Press of April 10, 1961:
We need to think not so much nationally or even in terms of greater economic co-operation between nations but in terms of wider groupings.
This is obviously, therefore, as the Prime Minister has indicated, a very important development. The relationship of our own country to that development is also one of major importance. Indeed, I think we will all agree that Canada's reaction should be a positive one, otherwise we may find ourselves carried along by events into an insufficient continentalism.
The Prime Minister also mentioned discussions about NATO. We on this side are only too anxious to support anything that can be done by our own government or by the other member governments, including the United Kingdom, to make that organization

stronger rather than weaker. The Prime Minister did not mention something that Mr. Macmillan himself also mentioned in Washington in his talks with President Kennedy, namely the desirability of a nuclear partnership inside NATO. I do not know whether that matter came up, but certainly it invites the question whether a nuclear partnership will make NATO stronger, or whether it may have the opposite effect of making it more difficult for NATO to strengthen its conventional forces.
Mention of NATO and the necessity of strengthening it reminds me of a statement made on this subject the day before yesterday by President de Gaulle, when he said, "It is the right and duty of the European continental powers to have a national defence that belongs to them". I hope, Mr. Speaker, that in any of the steps that are now being taken to strengthen NATO it will be made quite clear that there can be no salvation for the NATO countries in national defence alone.
The Prime Minister mentioned that they had a discussion about China. He said "The problem"-and it is a problem-"of Chinese representation at the United Nations is one that must be worked at against the next United Nations assembly". It would have been interesting, and perhaps we will learn later, to know the line which the Canadian government will be following in trying to work out a solution of that problem because, as the Prime Minister indicated, it is a problem that will certainly now come, perhaps in a concrete form, before the next United Nations assembly.
The Prime Minister mentioned uranium purchases. He is reported in the press as having said publicly "There is now a clear understanding of the position between the two governments in respect of this matter". He said that negotiations in regard to them- perhaps they should be called renegotiations -are about to take place shortly. In the face of negotiations which will be of such importance to Canada and to Canadian trade,
I do not desire to do or say anything which would complicate those negotiations. But surely the matter is, as the Prime Minister is reported to have said, quite clear. There is a commitment undertaken by the United Kingdom government. As the Minister of Trade and Commerce said not long ago, it is to be expected that the United Kingdom will honour that commitment, that the discussions to take place in London will confirm that commitment and discharge that undertaking so these orders can be allocated and bring new life, hope and activity to the uranium communities.
I am sure that the conversations which have just been concluded between the prime

I am equally sure that Mr. Macmillan has gone back to the United Kingdom confirmed in his view of the underlying friendship of the Canadian people not only to himself and his government but to the United Kingdom.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DISCUSSIONS WITH U.K. PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am certain that the visit to Canada of Prime Minister Macmillan was welcomed by all Canadians, and we are pleased that the Prime Minister has given to the house today something of a report, in general terms, of the discussion that took place between him and Prime Minister Macmillan. However, I think it would be fair to say that there was very little new in the statement made by the Prime Minister.
Certainly many questions are left very much unanswered. Not only are we still uncertain as to what facilities Canada will have for the export of her products to the United Kingdom market in the future, but in my opinion we are also very much up in the air as to the policy of the Canadian government in relation to the inner six, the outer seven and the Atlantic free trade area. We naturally hope that in any new developments Canada's rights will remain unimpaired, but we view with some misgiving the fact that Canada has not enunciated a clear policy of her own.
The Prime Minister made a very general reference to NATO. I am not really sure what it meant. The effect of his remarks was that there should be a strong, flexible and understanding partnership. The whole question of nuclear weapons for NATO, the question of the Polaris missile and so on, are unanswered. The position of our group is clear. We feel it would be a mistake to provide nuclear weapons for NATO at this time.

speechtext: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DISCUSSIONS WITH U.K. PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
The Canadian government has not made up its mind. The Leader of the Opposition went both ways. Hon. members may snicker, but at least we are able to say that we are opposed to nuclear weapons being placed in the hands of the NATO nations.
There was obviously no reference to economic development, because economic development under article 2 of the North Atlantic treaty is weak and almost forgotten. It is the O.E.C.D., the inner six, the outer seven and other means of bringing about economic cooperation which are now being put into effect in this field where NATO has failed.
The Prime Minister's reference to China and its possible admission to the United Nations at some future date was interesting but

Discussions with U.K. Prime Minister not very informative or clear. I am not certain what the position of the government is. I would hope his statement means that Canada will play a part in promoting the admission of China to the United Nations, because without China as a member disarmament talks are less useful and in our judgment it is more difficult for the United Nations to carry on its very valuable functions.
A general reference was made to the West Indies. We hope that in the future there can be closer co-operation between Canada and the West Indies in the economic and political fields. We hope that our immigration policies in the future will be tailored in such a way as to remove discrimination in this area.
The Prime Minister also made some reference to the uranium contracts. We hope that Canada will stand firm and insist that the United Kingdom honour the contracts for the purchase of 12,000 tons of uranium. We hope that these contracts will be allocated in a fair and generous way and that Eldorado will receive its fair share along with other companies so that the uranium industry of Canada and the communities affected will be maintained with as little dislocation as possible.
Undoubtedly the consultation between the Prime Minister of Canada and the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom has been welcome. Nonetheless we are disappointed that the Prime Minister has not been able to report accomplishments arising from this conference in a more concrete fashion.

I have had discussions with the cabinet in Prince Edward Island about crop insurance relating to potatoes in that province. I believe there have been reports

in the press that certain groups in Ontario are considering crop insurance in relation particularly to tobacco.

Under the cash advance legislation at the present time I believe that borrowers wishing to secure cash advances and unable to secure the endorsation of a landlord are unable to secure such advances. In some cases these people own land of their own, and I was wondering if new regulations could be brought in to enable such farmers to take advantage of these benefits with respect to the portion of land which they own.

This is a question which has been before the department on several occasions. There are some difficulties, of course, as the hon. members knows, in arriving at a formula which would meet these conditions. I have discussed the matter with the heads of various farm organizations in the hope that we can arrive at some formula which will meet the needs of those who are concerned in this way.

(Text):

The payments are not yet complete, but they are almost complete; there are just a few places still to be investigated. The totals up to April 5, 1961 are as follows: Manitoba, $649,537; Saskatchewan, $4,535,499; Alberta, $4,822,018; British Columbia, $90,035. Total for the four provinces under P.F.A.A., $10,097,000.

The Prairie Farm Assistance Act item which is before the committee now is an important one, and I think the statement the minister has made about the extent of crop insurance applications underlines the fact that crop insurance to date has been of very little real value. It certainly has not done a job for western producers in the crop insurance field in any way, and I think the results confirm the statements which were made by some of us on this side of the house that unless there is a major overhaul of the crop insurance legislation it is bound to remain ineffectual particularly in the higher risk areas of western Canada.
The minister has told us that last year 2,500 farmers had contracts in Manitoba and that this year perhaps 400 will have contracts in Saskatchewan, provided the government of which the hon. gentleman is a member decides to allow some pilot schemes in various parts of the province where fewer than 25 per cent of the farmers have signed crop insurance applications. Farmers in Alberta are

apparently not too interested in the legislation, because there is no scheme operating in that province at all.
If I remember correctly, the Canadian wheat board officials told us when they were before the agriculture committee that there are some 235,000 permit book holders in western Canada. So there are 235,000 farmers, and less than 3,000 of them have been covered by crop insurance. The best the minister could do today was to tell us that perhaps 5,000 or 6,000-2 per cent or 3 per cent of all the farmers in the prairie provinces-are going to avail themselves of crop insurance.
This government introduced the crop insurance scheme with a blaring of trumpets. This was to be another important plank in the magna carta for agriculture. Well, it is a pretty weak plank; very much of a sliver. It has been of a little use in Manitoba under particular conditions. In Saskatchewan, where I am informed the government, which has been promoting the scheme, sent out 40,000 application forms, the minister now says that 400 farmers have shown an interest. In other words, 1 per cent of the farmers receiving application forms have signed them and said they were interested.
Let us admit it; this is just a wee experimental project. This is not a system of crop insurance designed to protect western farmers. This is a little window dressing by the Conservative party with a few experimental projects under way. If I were in the position which the minister holds I would say that this scheme was a flop, a failure. It is not doing the job it was intended to do. I think I would be justified in using some of the strong language with regard to it which the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek used so effectively and, I am sure, so accurately in connection with another matter. The farmers he represents are not interested in crop insurance. I am sure of that. Most of the farmers I represent are not interested in crop insurance under this half-baked scheme which was brought in without prior consultation with the provinces.

Would the hon. member permit a question? The hon. member says the Saskatchewan government sent out 40,000 application forms. Does he know into which areas in Saskatchewan these forms were sent; into the high premium areas of hail or into the low premium areas?
I am not completely acquainted with what has been done-
Then you have made an irresponsible statement.

Not at all. I am willing to give the hon. member my impression of what has 90205-6-229i
Supply-Agriculture
been done there but I cannot guarantee its accuracy. My impression is that they were sent out to the low risk high yield areas and not to the high risk low yield areas. That is my impression although, as I say, I cannot guarantee the accuracy of it. I was reliably informed that there were 40,000 applications sent out. If the answer to the hon. member is correct then of course it means that the farmers who would be paying the small premiums rather than the larger ones would still not be interested in this scheme.
Will the hon. member allow a question?
Certainly.
Can you tell us how many municipalities applied that were turned down?

As I have said, I have no information in that regard, but the minister could give us that information. If the minister feels that the Saskatchewan government has not co-operated fully he can say so. I hope they have, and it is my impression that they have leaned over backward to try to get a crop insurance scheme working, and they are willing to co-operate.
I suggest that 20 per cent of the premium paid out of the national treasury is not enough. I remember how the Conservative members used to rip Jimmy Gardiner up and down the back and say he was a terrible minister of agriculture, but Jimmy Gardiner had legislation that functioned for many years. I refer to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. Under that system the provincial government did not have to pay at all. Approximately half of the losses have been paid over the years by the federal treasury and half by the farmers.

Would the hon. member permit a question? Does the hon. member for Assiniboia realize that Mr. Brown, a member of the Saskatchewan legislative assembly, last year in that assembly advocated very strongly that the provincial government should bring in a practical type of crop insurance scheme, and thought the farmers themselves should be the ones to judge whether or not it worked?

I do not know what that question has to do with this discussion. It is about as far removed from the Prairie Farm Assistance Act as that man in orbit was a couple of days ago. One individual in the Saskatchewan legislature made a speech and I am now being asked about it.
The crop insurance scheme, as a comprehensive scheme to protect western grain growers or for that matter the potato growers

Supply-Agriculture
of Prince Edward Island or the apple producers in the Okanagan, is not working. This represents just a few pilot plans which are not producing many results. The reason is very obvious. The federal government is backing away from the kind of responsibility it accepted under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. Under that act the federal government has been paying approximately 50 per cent of the losses, but under this scheme it is only prepared to pay 20 per cent of the premiums. They have scaled their responsibility down from 50 per cent to 20 per cent. One need not wonder why this does not work.
I suggest that the government should amend the Crop Insurance Act, and that its contribution should be increased at least to the 50 per cent level, the same level at which they were contributing under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. I feel if that were done it would provide at least some incentive to farmers to sign up; because of the subsequent reduction in the premiums. This would provide a more realistic acceptance of responsibility by the federal government.
I have never been strong in my support of crop insurance schemes, as I think my record in the house will show. I remember reading a report put out by the late R. F. Motherwell-he was a good friend of my mine at the university who did not agree with me politically in any way-in which he made very comprehensive findings. I think the main conclusion of his study was that for a long time we should be operating under a general crop protection scheme such as the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, with very definite and decided improvements in its application.
I would not like anyone to say that I am against a crop insurance act. On the contrary, I am in favour of it; but I 'feel we should give the farmers the opportunity to say whether they are getting adequate protection rather than giving them this half-baked scheme which appeals to just a handful of farmers on the prairies.
I feel that the payments made under prairie farm assistance are inadequate and outdated. These payments have not kept up in any way, shape or form with the increase to farmers in the cost of production. If one compares the benefits under prairie farm assistance today with the benefits received when the act was first introduced in the 1930's one will see that there is no question but that the payments under prairie farm assistance have much lower purchasing power than they did when the scheme was first initiated.
The benefit of prairie farm assistance has been allowed to slip and wither away over the years. Some improvements have been

made in the basis on which payments have been allocated. The hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek suggested yesterday that payments should be made on an individual basis. I have been advocating this policy for many years, but we have not succeeded in this regard. When I first came to parliament in 1945, 171 townships in Saskatchewan suffered crop failure. It was then declared a disaster area and the Prairie Farm Assistance Act began to function. As I understand it today, if one township is eligible then one half a township becomes an operating unit, and by splicing them to additional areas, smaller areas than half a township can be eligible.
I think you will find that 12 sections is the size.
Could the hon. member tell me which party brought this amendment into being?

There have been a great many amendments brought in over the years. Undoubtedly the Liberal party is responsible for more than the Conservative party, but it was here longer and had much greater opportunity to do so.
This party was responsible for the legislation in the first place.
I think you are right. It was first introduced in 1939. I might say, however, that we have all had a hand in this.
When were you in the government?

I have had a hand in many things even though I have not been in government. I remember when Jimmy Gardiner brought forward an amendment to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, and he was so opposed to socialism that he said farmers operating on crown land would not be allowed assistance under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. We had a difficult fight and it was hard going, but Jimmy pulled in his horns and decided he had gone a bit too far and gave the farmers operating on crown land a little better shake than he had initially intended to give them. He made some changes which I feel represented improvements to that act.
I suggest that it is now time to increase the payments under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act by a very substantial amount. If the payments were doubled the amount of money a farmer could receive as the result of a complete crop failure would not be a fantastic amount. It would be just $6 per acre providing his yield was less than three bushels per acre. We all realize that today, of course, with improved farming practices.

a yield of three bushels per acre is almost unheard of. Even with this proposed improvement a farmer with a crop failure, as defined in the act, would only receive a minimum guaranteed income. I feel there is room for both a crop insurance act and the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, but I suggest that it is now time to bring forward amendments to improve the application of these acts.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to put a question to the Minister of Agriculture. Has he had an official request from Quebec asking that the province take advantage of the crop insurance scheme implemented by the present government?
A great many farmers in the province of Quebec go in for special types of farming. In my own riding, for instance, it is tobacco farming. It would be of great interest to those farmers if the province of Quebec shared in this crop insurance scheme.
I should like to know whether the minister has received an official request from the provincial government.
(Text):

No, Mr. Chairman. I should just like to say a word about the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and crop insurance as related subjects. The policy of the government is to keep both the P.F.A.A. and the new legislation, crop insurance, in effect side by side. The Prairie Farm Assistance Act is a type of special measure to help farmers at a minimum cost in case of a drought in their area. Crop insurance is an altogether different thing. It is a fund set up by the farmers themselves on an actuarial basis so the individual farmer may insure himself against all types of risks due to weather. The amount of coverage will be 60 per cent of the actual value of production in the area, and farmers will soon realize that, over a period of years, for every 80 cents they put in they will receive back a dollar. It is not a form of social welfare or relief whatsoever; it is an individual insurance scheme carried out on an individual basis and on a sound actuarial plan.
For my own part I think I can say that wherever information pro and con has been put before farmers and questions have been allowed to be asked and answers given, the farmers in every case have supported crop insurance.
I should like to put on the record some of the discussion on this matter that took place in the legislature of Manitoba, as reported in the Hansard of that legislature of March 7, 1961. It is in effect, I think, a reply to the
Supply-Agriculture
hon. member for Assiniboia. These are quotations from a speech by Mr. Hutton, the minister of agriculture:
The crop insurance program I would say, is a success in Manitoba in 1960, and indications are that it's going to be successful in 1961. We are enlarging two of the areas; another one will be set up; it will be announced in the house. We are extending crop insurance to the beet growers in Manitoba.
I am leaving out some interjections which I do not think add to or subtract from what the minister said. I continue:
Our experiment has been confined to areas representing about 20 per cent of the province of Manitoba. We have learned a great deal; we have come a long way in terms of getting information. Sooner than you wish to think we'll be in a position to offer crop insurance to the whole province of Manitoba. I think they're going to find out that as we said here in Manitoba that it's an educational program.
Then he went on to discuss classification of land and that sort of thing in connection with the crop insurance program. If hon. members will read the press clippings across Canada they will see that in Prince Edward Island the government mentioned crop insurance in the speech from the throne and declared their intention of bringing in a scheme for tobacco and potatoes. If hon. members read the press clippings from Alberta they will see that the farm organizations, knowing of the existing federal legislation, are asking their government to take positive action to bring crop insurance to Alberta. If hon. members will talk to the fruit producers of the province of British Columbia, the minister of agriculture, or any of those other people who are definitely interested in crop insurance under the present set-up, they will see that the provinces are moving forward under crop insurance not only with respect to cereal crops in the three prairie provinces but also in the specialty crops all across Canada. I would predict that in the next few years every province in Canada, with the possible exception of Newfoundland, about which I am not too clear at the moment, will have crop insurance schemes, and as those schemes demonstrate their soundness on an actuarial basis they will spread to all regions of every province. I believe that before a decade is over hon. members will see crop insurance schemes widely in effect over all the agricultural areas of Canada. It is good legislation.

I should like to make a few comments on this particular item. First, there has been some hold-up in the province of Alberta with respect to P.F.A.A. payments this year. I hope the department has got around this particular snag in the

Supply-Agriculture
administration of this part of the act and that the cheques will continue to go out to farmers in the east central part of Alberta particularly.
I should like to say I am disappointed that the Alberta government has not made some move to adopt a system of crop insurance. Certainly in the western part of Alberta, particularly, where there is a great threat of hail, the crop insurance plan envisioned by this government and passed in 1958 or 1959 would be of benefit to those farmers. It would at least reduce their losses considerably.
The hon. member for Assiniboia went to great lengths to explain his theory of prairie farm assistance. He also showed his ignorance of the legislation, which did not really surprise me but may have surprised some hon. members. He spoke about areas eligible to qualify and said that it was a township. Actually this has been reduced to 12 sections. If he cares to read his own remarks in Hansard of a couple of years ago, after this government amended the Prairie Farm Assistance Act to a considerable extent, he will find that he complimented the government for doing so. It was one of those rare occasions when the hon. member for Assiniboia found himself in an agreeable frame of mind. He complimented the government on bringing in the amendments and said he certainly thought they would do away with many of the complaints he had received with respect to prairie farm assistance at that time. Today he has made another request. He has said that the payments should be increased. This is an old story coming from him. He is continually wanting increased payments of one kind or another.
Hear, hear.

But again he shows his ignorance of the operations of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. He said the payments should be doubled; they should be increased to $6. If the payments were doubled they would be increased to $8.
The hon. member is right. I made a mistake; the lowest payment is $4 an acre.

I compliment the hon. member on being in such an agreeable mood that he admits he made a mistake. I point out these two mistakes he made with regard to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. I hope the committee will look at all his remarks in the way I have done and question every one of them and look for his errors in most of them. I can find some most of the time.
Under this item can the minister explain the significance of the section marked with

an "(S)", where there is an increase of $6,800,000 in the amount of carrying costs of temporary wheat reserves?

Mr. Chairman, I did not catch the answer given by the Minister of Agriculture to the member for Joliette-L'As-somption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) who asked whether the Quebec government had requested that the province be allowed to take advantage of this legislation on crop insurance. I do not know whether the minister has answered that question-
He said no.

The minister said no. In that case, I ask him whether the government which preceded that of Mr. Lesage had made that request? I believe it did not, for the legislation could not be applied in the province of Quebec, as we pointed out to the minister while we were considering the measure. We had, however, submitted suggestions and proposals which were not agreed to.
That is why the province of Quebec is not interested, any more than Ontario and the eastern provinces are interested.
I am glad to hear the minister say that, within two years, the provinces will share in the crop insurance scheme. We are noting his words; they will remain graven in our memories and two years hence, we shall be happy to congratulate the minister if this legislation is implemented throughout Canada.
By the same token, I venture to predict that, unless the act is amended, there will be no possibility of applying it in eastern Canada.
(Text):

Mr. Chairman, with respect to the same subject, I should like the Minister of Agriculture to tell the committee how many provinces have taken advantage of this legislation. The act was passed about two years ago, and the government's contribution under the legislation has amounted to almost nothing because all it pays is 20 per cent of the premiums and half the cost of administration. It is only a matter of a loan to the province of up to 75 per cent of the amount if the loss is above $200,000, and if the loss is below $200,000 the federal government and the provincial government do not pay a cent. In addition, we know that at least 25 per cent of the farmers have to join in making an application under the crop insurance legislation, and the governments concerned will never pay more than 60 per cent of the loss. There are so many conditions to be fulfilled before the legislation can be taken advantage

of that I believe the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska is right when he says that ten years from now there will not be two provinces that will have taken advantage of it. I should like to know from the minister how many provinces now take advantage of this legislation, which has been in effect for two years.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, before we hear the comments of the Minister of Agriculture, may I be permitted to say that, while it is true that the Quebec government is not interested in coming under this crop insurance scheme, Quebec farmers, for their part, are indeed interested, especially those who go in for specialized farming; I refer to the people in my area who grow cigar, pipe and cigarette tobacco and who suffer considerable losses almost every year due to frost and drought.
I ask the provincial government to co-operate and to help those specialized growers of cigar, pipe and cigarette tobacco, especially so because the present government is not doing anything for specialized farmers. As a matter of fact, grants for the construction of greenhouses and driers have been abolished in Quebec. That is why I ask the Quebec government to co-operate with the federal government in helping out farmers who grow crops of that kind. It is high time the provincial government did something for Quebec farmers instead of discarding the policies adopted by the former provincial government.
Why didn't the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm speak along that line at the time his good friend, Mr. Barrette, was in power?
He was of greater assistance to cigarette, cigar and pipe tobacco producers than is the present provincial government.

Mr. Chairman, I never heard the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm speak on this subject before; he has been mute as a fish about it, although he had an interest in the matter because the Joliette area includes a large section where cigarette tobacco is grown.
The hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm who, I think, has been parliamentary secretary to the minister who later became premier, was in a better position than anyone else here to urge the provincial government to meet with the federal authorities, to call personally upon 25 per cent of the cigarette tobacco growers to meet with Mr. Barrette-the close friend of the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm -and ask them to come to Ottawa to meet

with the Minister of Agriculture. Since the latter is a friend of the hon. member for J oliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm,	something
might have been achieved. But he did not do anything. This legislation is hard or even impossible to apply and, as the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm has just personally admitted, if the provincial government does nothing about it, then it is up to the federal government to do something for the farmers.
If the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm reads the act, he will find that the federal government does not deal with individuals. And what about autonomy?
You do not know anything. (Text):

Mr. Chairman, I think I should say a few words on the question of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and crop insurance, after what has been said by the hon. member for Assiniboia. He made one statement that I think was quite factual, namely "I have never been too strongly in favour of crop insurance and my record shows it". I believe the government of the province of Saskatchewan can be looked upon in the same way. They were strongly in favour of crop insurance during the years when there was a Liberal government at Ottawa which did not bring such legislation before parliament. The government of that province changed its tune after we enacted crop insurance legislation.
The minister of agriculture of the province of Saskatchewan indicated last fall, when speaking to the delegates to the annual meeting of the Saskatchewan wheat pool, that the provincial government was not too interested in going ahead with the plan. About a week later he changed his mind and the statement was made that they would have proceeded with a scheme and would have proceeded sooner but the federal legislation had been passed too late for them to commence action prior to the end of the session of their legislature.
I have here some of the forms used in the province of Saskatchewan by the provincial government to promote, if you can call it promotion, a crop insurance plan there. First of all I want to say that in many areas of the province P.F.A.A. will continue to be the most effective instrument to ensure a reasonable standard of living for the people in those areas. However, there are other areas that have never been able to qualify under P.F.A.A., although in some cases farmers who

Sup p ly-A griculture
have suffered crop failures have had to contribute to the fund over a period of years through their sales of grain and the 1 per cent levy.
If you take some of the good townships in the northern part of my riding around Kinis-tino the cost of crop insurance is $1 per acre, of which amount the federal government is providing 20 cents. The saving on the P.F.A.A. levy on a 20-bushel crop is approximately 25 cents per acre. The hail insurance rate is around 30 cents, which makes a total of 55 cents. That leaves a balance of 25 cents per acre to be picked up by the farmers in order that they may enjoy an all-risk crop insurance plan. It is my belief that even on that basis it would be in the interests of many of them to come under this program and see if it will work to their advantage.
But the significant thing is that the province of Saskatchewan has not contributed a single cent to the crop insurance plan, although that government have advocated it almost since they first took office.
The province is paying half the administration costs.

Half the administration costs but no other charge whatsoever. I think that is one of the things the hon. member for Assiniboia should remember. After all, the provincial government has a responsibility in these areas and it is not assuming that responsibility today. It is my belief that the province can very well afford to pay 10 per cent of the cost, and I believe the balance of 15 cents per acre is an amount the farmers would be glad to pay in order to have crop insurance in the good crop areas of our province.

Mr. Chairman, the last speech we have heard underlines what has been a suspicion of mine all the time; that the members of the Conservative party in the house want to dump into the laps of the provinces the responsibility which the federal government accepted under P.F.A.A. The statement has been made that the provincial treasury of Saskatchewan should pay a certain proportion of the cost of the crop insurance plan, and this emphasizes exactly what some of us have been saying for many years. We think the Prairie Farm Assistance Act is the place where improvements should be made.
As has been pointed out, the largest payment that can be made under the act is $4 per acre with a yield up to three bushels per acre. I would ask the minister to tell us how many farmers received payments in the last year for which he has figures in each of the categories under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. My impression is that a very tiny proportion of farmers received the largest payment.

Therefore if one were to double the amount of payment a farmer who receives $2 an acre now on half the cultivated acreage up to 400 acres, or $400, would get $800 and this would still represent a small part of his general cost of production.
These payments would be higher than those for the lower yield categories. I suggest it is still a very small part or a relatively small proportion of the farmer's main operating expenses. I do not think that crop insurance should be loaded onto the provinces. I have no objection if a province wants to make a payment; that is fine. I think the Saskatchewan government has set up a reserve fund, in case of a widespread crop failure in which case funds would be made available by the provincial treasury.
Another thing the hon. member for Ros-thern failed to point out is that under this scheme the provincial government sustains full liability for the losses. This government does not guarantee 20 per cent of the losses at all; it guarantees 20 per cent of the premiums. If there were one or two widespread crop failures in the early operation of a crop insurance scheme that was in general use, the liability for payments out of the provincial treasury would be of absolutely fantastic proportions. The province of Saskatchewan would go bankrupt if there were widespread crop failures, as there were in the thirties, and on the assumption that most of the farmers were in a crop insurance scheme. The provincial government has a definite commitment and a definite liability under the act as it has been drafted.

I believe that Manitoba's crop insurance scheme worked very well last year. I understand that the number of those to be covered this year is going to be doubled. However, I should like to ask the minister whether the premiums charged by the province of Manitoba were sufficient to cover crop losses, how much the scheme has cost the federal government and how much it has cost the provincial government?

While we are looking up the figures, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say briefly that last year was a fairly good crop year and the surplus on the basis of premiums was very large. If my memory serves me correctly, the losses were $92,000 and the premiums came to over $300,000. That is in a fairly good crop year. If that fund were to build up over a period of years the province of Manitoba plans to reduce the premium in order to keep it strictly on a cost basis and to give inducement to farmers to keep the act working well and not to abuse it.

I wonder whether I might correct a statement I made yesterday to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam when he asked about the number of townships where no P.F.A.A. had been paid. I said I did not have the figures but that if my memory served me from a discussion of some time ago, there was just a handful of those townships. We have been examining the figures more carefully overnight and the correct figures in the last 21 years are as follows. In Manitoba 63 townships had never received a payment. In Saskatchewan 17 had never received a payment. In Alberta the figure is 51. If those figures are added together, out of approximately 7,000 you get a total of 131 townships that have not received any payment in 21 years.
I never heard anything quite as ridiculous as the statement made by the hon. member for Assiniboia when he suggests that we double the levies for P.F.A.A. in order to double the payments.
I never said any such thing.
All that would do in the good crop areas in our province would be to make a farmer with a 20 bushel crop pay 50 cents for something that he could not get.
Speaking on the point of order, may I say that I made no such statement as that which the hon. member alleges I made.
The hon. member knows very well that if you double the payment you will have to double the levy. Where is the money going to come from otherwise?
They do not go together at all.

They certainly do go together. All I want to say further in that regard is this. Crop insurance and P.F.A.A. are two distinct things and they will serve people in distinct areas as well. I certainly think that trying to say they are both one and the same thing is not shedding any light on the subject.

I want to deny very definitely that I said the contributions of producers should be doubled. I made no such statement. I would ask the minister whether he can give the committee the number of farmers that received prairie farm assistance in the last year under the various yield categories?

This is for the
crop year 1960-61. From zero to three bushels, 2,515; from three bushels to five bushels, 5,226; from five bushels to eight bushels, 26,334; or a total of 34,077.

I should like to ask the minister a question on a different topic, if 1 may. I am aware that the minister has
Supply-Agriculture
been plagued with many requests in regard to permit books. I wonder whether he has given any consideration to transferring the handling of permit books from the wheat board to P.F.A.A.? The reason I ask that question is this. I believe that the P.F.A.A. officials have more detailed information with regard to all the land on the prairie than have the officials of the wheat board and that it would be much easier for them with their set-up to look after the issuing of permit books.

I want to raise an objection to the statement that has been made by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek. I would think that this would be a very retrograde step. I think that the farmers have much greater faith and confidence in the wheat board officials than they have in the prairie farm assistance officials. The prairie farm assistance people in the past, under the Liberal government, were in the main only liberal Liberals. The ones I knew were Liberals and party hacks too. They picked up some dough from the P.F.A.A. and then when an election was on you were not sure whether they were travelling for P.F.A.A., Mr. Gardiner's department, or whether they were trying to elect some broken down Liberal candidate.
Oh, oh.
It is different now.
Someone says that it is different now. Now they try to elect broken down Tory candidates.
No such thing.
You will not get any broken down C.C.F.'ers.
I do not know what one might take from that statement.
The obvious logical conclusion.

I think it would be a mistake to take the issuance of permit books out of the hands of the wheat board and place it in the hands of the prairie farm assistance people in the provinces. I know of no farm organization that has asked for this to be done; at least I have not seen that they have asked for it. I can see no advantage that would come from it and I can see a great many disadvantages.

The hon. member for Assiniboia said he took exception to the statement I made. I do not see any exception. The appointments of the officials of the wheat board, P.F.R.A. and P.F.A.A. are all made by the same people and on the same basis.

Supply-Agriculture

That is news to me. I thought the wheat board appointed its own people and I believe that it does so. However, I think the minister is pretty much in control of the people appointed by P.F.A.A. However, I have much more confidence in the officials appointed by the Canadian wheat board because I think there is much less of partisan politics there than there is in P.F.A.A.

If the hon. gentleman has something more on this vote he can go ahead because I was going to ask for the indulgence of the committee.
What is this item "appropriations not required for 1961-62" on page 8?
We have not yet come to that item. We have not yet passed this item, have we?
No. That is statutory.

Mr. Chairman, I rise in connection with item No. 36, the administration of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. I am rising basically on a question of privilege.
I wish to indicate to the committee the views of the Prime Minister when he sat on the opposition side of the house. I will quote just one short extract from Hansard. This extract is to be found at page 208 of Hansard for 1950.
Mr. Chairman, could we find out what is the question of privilege before the hon. member reads this extract?
I am referring to section 12 of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.
Yes; but what about it?

I am coming to the point. The Prime Minister said:
The attitude that an opposition is something to put up with on occasion is prevalent in some quarters.
Then he went on to say:
If the cabinet is to be trusted; if we are to accept at face value what ministers say, then we had better all be absent from this house.
Then a little later on he said:
I know that cabinets long in power tend to believe that they rule by divine right; I know that they do not welcome oppositions, but a one-party state is not a democratic state.
Since the new ministry came into office the rights of parliament have been noted and commented upon. I wish to quote briefly from the Victoria Daily Times of February 20, 1960. The title of the article is, " 'Restoring' Parliament". The article reads:
When the Conservatives-

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has so far not laid any basis for a question of privilege. He has merely read extracts from Hansard, and he now wants to read an article from a newspaper.
I think it is important that he should first lay the basis for his question of privilege, and if you rule that there is a question of privilege, the hon. member may proceed to take it up. The hon. member mentioned section 12 of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, but then he read something that was said several years ago.

My question of privilege involves the obligation of the minister to provide all members of parliament, including those in the opposition, with information that is available to him in the form of an annual report.
I can sum up this editorial in one sentence. It says:
Mr. Diefenbaker used to charge the Liberals with submerging the rights of parliament in a sea of autocracy.
On Tuesday night I raised a question in the estimates of the minister with respect to the vote concerning the board of grain commissioners for Canada. I say that it is not accidental that within a few hours of our disposing of that vote the minister tabled- as is indicated in Votes and Proceedings of yesterday-when our debate had concluded on Tuesday night, the annual report of the board of grain commissioners for Canada.
I say that it is another instance of arrogance to table this report only yesterday. I say that it cannot simply be a coincidence that this report dealing with the activities under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act is tabled in this way.
I have not yet received it.
Oh, come now.

I am making this charge, and I am making it very seriously. We saw this disregard of the present small opposition in the first session of parliament after this government received this massive support.
By the people of Canada.
By the people of Canada, yes; but I remind you of what the Prime Minister of this country had to say about the rights of an opposition, no matter how small.
When he was in opposition.

When he was in opposition. I have had only a few minutes to check this matter, but my recollection starts with the first session of this parliament. The first estimates passed in the House of Commons that session as I recall were the estimates of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. We spent several days discussing those estimates. In that case with too obvious stupidity the government did not delay even two or three days. I think on the day following the passing of all the hon. lady's departmental items the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration presented, in the manner I have indicated, the annual report for her department which report then became public.
On two occasions the Minister of Labour, in matters relating to information on unemployment has followed this practice. Within a day after he was no longer responsible to this house for debate and questioning he filed information that had also been asked for, I assume, by government backbenchers who are interested in unemployment, too. This information would have been as helpful to them as it was necessary to the opposition before the debate was concluded.
Last year, in connection with the Department of Agriculture again, I was interested in this matter and I recall-

Mr. Chairman, I think these remarks of the hon. member would be better stated at another time. The hon. member has strayed quite a way from the subject that is under consideration at this moment.

We have before us the estimates of the Department of Agriculture. I think the Minister of Agriculture is anxious to dispose of his estimates, as always are all ministers. I have not abused the privilege of criticizing his estimates. It is to my mind more than a coincidence to find this sort of thing happening again and again.
I would refer to another item from the same department. This incident occurred last year when the department was under the

Sup p ly-A griculture
former minister. We had a very important discussion about relief to the western grain growers for crops which had not been harvested and were left under the snow, and a bill was introduced to provide some relief under those circumstances. I took an active part in that debate. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate as another former prairie dweller was equally interested. Indeed, he happened to be in Winnipeg during the debate and I remember that as my deskmate he told me when he came back that he had heard the minister of agriculture for the province of Manitoba say certain things with respect to the attitude of the provincial department of agriculture with regard to this emergency legislation for the prairie grain growers at that time.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate after his return immediately put on the order paper a request for the tabling of correspondence between the minister of agriculture in Manitoba and the federal Minister of Agriculture because, naturally, he wanted to ascertain whether the minister of agriculture in Manitoba was putting in writing and letting the federal Minister of Agriculture know the same views as he was voicing publicly in the legislature on the day the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was in the gallery of the legislature. There was no particular shortage of time. My recollection is-and I think I am right because I made a note about it at the time-that again within hours after that debate was concluded the government tabled the correspondence between the two ministers. I say that certainly this provides no evidence of remedy relating to the hullabaloo which the Prime Minister of this country raised when he was in opposition, because I do not think that this ministry can give any examples of any similar disregard for parliament so blatant as those which I have just illustrated.
On the point of order, if I may say a word-
I think I might be able to save a lot of time-

On the question which has been raised, I think the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River is, generally, correct. I did not raise it yesterday although I was tempted to do so and perhaps I should have raised it.
Too late.

I refer to the fact that the report of the board of grain commissioners was tabled after we had begun to discuss the item. I think this is a very bad practice. I think it is not only an unparliamentary practice but a somewhat cowardly practice not to make the report available to hon. members

well in advance so that they can intelligently discuss the item involved instead of waiting until the item is called and then hurrying to table the report.
I do not want to put words which he did not use into the mouth of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, but if I correctly interpret what he said he complained that the report relating to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act has been just tabled-
No. My information is that it was tabled yesterday.
For what year?

For the crop year ending
1959-60.

Well, I think the hon. gentleman is in error. I have here sessional paper No. 12, the report of the activities under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act for the crop year 1959-60 and according to the information on the front cover it was tabled on December 2, 1960, so I believe the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River is in error as far as this publication is concerned. However, he was quite accurate as far as the report of the board of grain commissioners is concerned. The government is only half as bad as he has pointed out. But he still has a very good case.

The hon. member for Assiniboia was hardly on a point of order but he has said what I was going to say, namely that the report in question was tabled several months ago. This can be confirmed by a study of Votes and Proceedings, for Friday, December 2. I will read it:
By Mr. Hamilton (Qu'Appelle), a member of the Queen's privy council, -Report on activities under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act for the crop year, ended July 31, 1960, pursuant to section 12 of the said act, chapter 213, R.S.C. 1952.
However, I think there is a point in connection with the remarks of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River which has not been brought out. It is not a question of the department not fulfilling its functions under the legislation. That is done as rapidly as it can be done, because the machinery is all laid on. The trouble may be this, and it may apply to this matter of the report of the grain commissioners. There is a distribution list which was set up, I suppose, long before many of us came here, and the distribution list provides only 100 copies for the House of Commons. I think that what actually happens is that those responsible for the distribution presume that certain hon. members get these copies and others do not. I imagine, of course, copies will go to the library. But I can assure the committee that the minute the report of the board of grain commissioners came into my hands it was tabled. There were no

instructions on my part to delay it, because there is nothing in that report to cause embarrassment to anybody. However, I think that the hon. member possibly has a point, and I will look into it. As far as my department is concerned, if there is a limited distribution that may be what has caused the trouble.

I thank the minister for his statement, but that is not what caused my protest in so far as the annual report of the board of grain commissioners is concerned. The minister knows that on or before the day required by statute the department must file with the Clerk of the House of Commons a master copy of the report. That master copy, as indicated on page 433 of Votes and Proceedings of Wesdnesday, was only then filed. I will read the relevant entry:
By Mr. Hamilton (Qu'Appelle), a member of the Queen's privy council-Report for 1960 of the Board of Grain Commissioners for Canada.
That is quite irrespective of how many copies are available subsequently for distribution at the request of members who, having read that notice, wish to examine that particular document further. So, in particular, the explanation of the minister is invalid respecting the tabling officially and for the first time with the Clerk of the house of such a report. It was tabled within hours after we had let the minister off the hook in debate, as it were, on this item, having no further questions to ask on the board of grain commissioners-

On a question of accuracy, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has made a serious mistake here because the vote on the item concerning the board of grain commissioners was not taken until long after this document was tabled. The report was available in the committee. I saw several members with it in their possession and the statement which the hon. member has now made that first the item went through and then the report was tabled is not true.
I was in the committee all Tuesday night, and if one looks at Hansard one will find that the vote was carried and, subsequently, the following day, this report was tabled.

No. I am sorry, but I must correct the hon. member. The vote was not carried Tuesday night. The chairman will be able to say exactly when it was carried, because he keeps a record. But if the hon. member examines Hansard he will find it was carried yesterday.

I recollect that now. 1 accept that.
