Your batting average is not too good today.

My point is still valid. The only notice available to a member of the House of Commons that this report had been tabled would have been the receipt in his mail box today, Thursday, of yesterday's Votes and Proceedings. It would otherwise not be possible to know that this report was filed with the Clerk yesterday, the same day on which the debate was finished.
With respect to tabling the report under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act I simply want to repeat that I have been in my seat since 2.30 this afternoon. While here I sent for the last available report under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. A note came back with the report to the effect that it was tabled yesterday. I excuse the staff completely because I am sure that the individuals concerned had in mind an inquiry I had made before coming to the chamber in respect of the other agricultural report, namely the report of Board of Grain Commissioners for Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask for the indulgence of the committee but if it is not forthcoming I will not proceed. I was not here yesterday when the minister was good enough to reply to an inquiry made in respect of the Fairford river development in Manitoba. There was one point in his answer about which I should like to have a little further elucidation. I understood from his answer that this work is being carried out by the government of Manitoba but the federal government is paying half the cost. Could the minister tell us whether this is being done under some general policy or whether it is an ad hoc arrangement in respect of this project alone? My recollection is that under the legislation that was previously in force there was a 374-37-1-25 arrangement for the division of the cost of projects of this sort. I wonder if there is some new general policy, and I would like the minister to explain to what categories of project it would be applicable.

For the last several years

at least five or six-a policy has been developing in regard to the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act where certain projects are carried out on a joint basis by the provincial and federal governments. The item to which the hon. member refers is included in item No. 33 but in the heading above it will be seen that this item includes the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act program, land protection and reclamation and development. This program has been evolving over a period of years, but this is part of the regular program.

Supply-Agriculture
This is, in other words, applicable over the entire area covered by the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act for any project in which the federal government sees fit to participate?

Yes, but in the
case of Newfoundland we make grants to the government of that province, which looks after its own projects. I have forgotten the exact amount of the grant in respect of the bog land development.
Is this a similar formula to that applied in respect of the maritime marshlands?

No, it is a
different operation entirely. This is a grant we have given in respect of bog land development and it happens to be included under this vote.

The minister was good enough to concede that reports of the kind to which I have referred should be tabled in the house as soon as available. I wonder whether he would make inquiries to find out when the printed report of the Board of Grain Commissioners for Canada was first made available by the Queen's printer, and endeavour in the future to see that this type of report is not simply tabled after the opportunity for debate has passed but as soon as possible.

Item agreed to.
21. Special grant to Pacific national exhibition, Vancouver, $200,000.

The minister indicated yesterday, as will be seen at page 3542 of Hansard, that he would be prepared to make some further comment in regard to this item. I believe the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard also had some remarks to make in this regard.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words about this particular grant.
Does the minister now have three parliamentary secretaries?

I would first like to say that this grant is most welcome to the people of Vancouver but it is unfortunate that Vancouver, at the present time, has no suitable coliseum. If it had I would certainly not comment in this vein today. The people of Vancouver urgently need a coliseum as well as a livestock building. However, under the present situation we will perhaps not get either.
I should like to refer to a letter which the minister sent me regarding this subject, because it pretty well sets out the objectives he

has in mind in connection with the building. The minister stated in his letter of February 20, 1961, as follows:
We have recognized that the accommodation for livestock at the P.N.E. is inadequate for an exhibition of its size and for the livestock which it attracts to its shows. This applies not only to the accommodation for cattle but, probably of greater importance, to the show ring and judging facilities. We have, therefore, undertaken to assist the exhibition to establish more adequate accommodation.
Mr. Chairman, obviously the minister had in mind adequate accommodation for a livestock show. Later in the letter he indicates how the building is to be financed through the provision, in these estimates, of the sum of $200,000. He further states in the letter as follows:
I have heard that there has been some controversy in Vancouver in connection with a sports coliseum equipped with ice facilities. In the Department of Agriculture, obviously, we have no Interest in a building for that purpose.
-But any funds provided by this department would be devoted only to the needs of the livestock show.
I presume that the minister feels the contribution of $200,000 will be a major contribution toward the construction of a mink, cat and dog show building, but I wish to inform the minister that in actuality this money will be devoted to a livestock building with some 8,000 seats capable of being used mainly as a hockey arena. The minister has said that this building should be used primarily for agricultural purposes.
I am also informed that in 1959-60 there was a submission made by the Pacific national exhibition that this grant of $200,000 would be insufficient to construct the building.
On December 12, 1960 the minister replied to that submission, stating as follows:
I am disturbed by the impression conveyed in the submission of September 12 that subsequent funds might be made available by the federal government to a total of $1 million.
If the Pacific national exhibition requires $1 million, and I suggest that it does, then that organization is not really building a livestock building but is building a large, needed coliseum. That is the point I wanted to put forward today. While the minister wants to help the people of Vancouver he really wants to contribute to the construction of a livestock building but he is actually contributing to the construction of a coliseum. Unfortunately we cannot agree in Vancouver as to where the coliseum should be built. If this must be tied to agriculture we will not have the coliseum we need and the building will not be placed where we want it.
The Pacific national exhibition board, and it is an excellent one, certainly has indicated in some of its directives what it proposed, and

this indication appears in some of its literature dated March 1 last where the following is stated:
The second stage provided installation of an ice plant to serve hockey and other events as well as heating equipment for the building. The city was being asked to advance $280,000 in 1960 and a similar amount in 1961. The province would be asked to contribute a similar amount as the city. It was understood $280,000 will be forthcoming from the federal government, while the P.N.E. is putting up $450,000.
The mayor who presided over the affairs of Vancouver in 1958 wrote to us here in Ottawa about this proposed building, and no mention is made in his entire letter of any building being constructed for livestock purposes. The mayor of the day talks about a contribution of a million dollars toward a coliseum. In his letter he said:
To assist in these considerations would you kindly advise if your government will still make the million dollar grant to the city for this coliseum, particularly if the project were developed in the downtown area, or would the former requirement still stand, i.e. the coliseum must be in conjunction with the operation of the exhibition.
From what I have said, after perusing some of the documents of the Pacific national exhibition and after giving consideration to the mayor's letter, it is obvious that the real requirement of the city at this time is a coliseum and not so much-although this is incidental-a livestock building. This impression is left most clearly when you peruse the many newspaper articles which have appeared over the last four or five years when consideration was given to this proposed building.
When I close my remarks I wonder whether the minister will indicate that in 1956 the federal government made an offer of $1 million to the Pacific national exhibition. If the offer was made, will the minister indicate who made the offer on behalf of the federal government and to whom was it made? I hope the minister realizes that a change has taken place in the situation since the federal offer, that is, the proposed offer, was made in 1956. At that time the government stipulated it could make a grant only to assist an agricultural fair, which tied the coliseum to the Pacific national exhibition grant. Since 1956 the voters have voted upon that issue and they rejected a million dollar bylaw to cover the city's share of a coliseum on the Pacific national exhibition ground. No longer can a coliseum be judged solely as an adjunct of an agricultural fair.
The building is needed today not only as a place for conventions and sports events but as a public works project, which is so much needed in the Vancouver area at the present time. I am not going to take up the time of the committee by referring to other newspaper articles, but I should like the minister
Supply-Agriculture
to comment upon what was said by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond yesterday when he discussed whether this building could be erected in the downtown area, or whether a downtown coliseum could be used for agricultural purposes, just as much as one in the Pacific national exhibition ground, which obviously operates for only a short time in the year.
The other real point, Mr. Chairman, is the fact that the grant by the department at this time could make possible a proper building for proper purposes erected where the city desires to build it, and apparently that would be in the downtown area.
The courses open in connection with this much discussed building would be, (a) withhold the grant for the time being, a thing which obviously nobody wants because they need the money out there; or, (b) make the grant now, with the condition that no ice refrigeration be installed for five years, which would take the hockey element out of the building. If such a condition were attached then, of course, I feel that the proposed plans would be reduced considerably and immediately and we would then end up with a proper livestock building instead of ending up with a combined livestock and coliseum building, which will be too small and will not be where the people want it.
Another suggestion would be for the minister to consider making a matching grant with the Minister of Trade and Commerce of at least $1 million so that we could have a proper building for conventions, trade shows and agricultural events, and a building in which we could celebrate our birthday centennial in 1967. That is another course that is open.
There is a feeling that in 1956 an offer of $1 million was made. If that is true, then I presume the minister could once again make an offer on behalf of this government or, with the Minister of Trade and Commerce, he could make a grant available larger than this item of $200,000.
I also notice that there was an item in the estimates which indicated that the Canadian national exhibition was to receive a sum of $500,000 from the federal government during the present fiscal year. Therefore, it would appear that the minister has some discretion over the amount to be voted.
I think the minister is aware of the fact that the city of Vancouver owns the Pacific national exhibition, and it is the same city which proposed to erect a building either there or in the downtown area. If adequate funds were made available then, of course, we could have agricultural events take place in the building and other events could also take place there.

Supply-Agriculture
Probably the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond will be asking some questions on the same item. I think I have covered the situation pretty well. I hope that the money can be made available and in the right quantity in order that we will end up with the right kind of building that is so badly needed in the area at this time.

Before the minister replies, I should like to make one or two remarks to supplement those already made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard.
First, I should like to emphasize to the minister that we in the Vancouver area sincerely appreciate very much this $200,000 grant. I would emphasize that it is urgently needed at the present time for a show ring out at the Pacific national exhibition.
The point that I wish to bring to the minister's attention, and one which I think the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard was trying to draw to his attention, is that in 1967 we shall be celebrating our centennial. I wonder whether the minister could give serious consideration to the addition of $800,000, perhaps by way of a supplementary estimate, to make up a $1 million grant to the Pacific national exhibiton.
I suggest that perhaps he could, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard has said, also co-operate with the Department of Trade and Commerce and provide a further $1 million. Perhaps I seem a little bit generous in throwing around millions of dollars, but in item No. 36, which was just passed, we voted some $49 million for the storage of surplus grain. Over the years since 1956 some $200 million has been used for the storage of grain. Perhaps I could say in a humorous way that we would be prepared to have a building for at least the temporary storage of grain if we could participate in some of the moneys voted under item No. 36. But I would point out to the minister that the very progressive Minister of Trade and Commerce has already provided some $300,000 for the Seattle trade fair in 1961 and I have been particularly pleased with the progressive attitude that the new Minister of Agriculture has taken in trying to assist in agricultural matters. I feel that if he could produce this $1 million and make a start toward this agricultural building or agricultural coliseum, which would have a seating capacity of 15,000 and could be used for many other events, the minister would receive the gratitude both of myself and the people of Vancouver generally.

Mr. Chairman, as a governor of the Pacific national exhibition I think it is my duty to say a word about this grant of $200,000. The grant was originally given for

the purpose of assisting the livestock business of British Columbia and as the grant comes from the Department of Agriculture I presume it can be used only for exhibition purposes on the exhibition grounds. I do not think I have anything more to say about the matter. We all know there has been a controversy involving the businessmen of Vancouver with respect to having a coliseum in the centre of Vancouver rather than having a livestock building on the grounds of the Pacific national exhibition. To me it is absolutely ridiculous to talk about locating the coliseum in the centre of Vancouver and moving cows, horses, sheep, swine, chickens and everything to the centre of the city just because that is where the building is. After all is said and done, the Pacific national exhibition grounds are only two or three miles from the centre of Vancouver and I suggest that if there is too much controversy over this whole matter the minister may even change his mind and not provide a grant at all, which I hope will not happen.

Mr. Chairman, as found on page 3542 of Hansard, the minister indicated that he would make some further comment. I hope the item will not pass without the minister making some suitable comment, perhaps only to indicate that he is going to give us the $1 million.

The minister is always very canny when local issues are being discussed. The last official word we had from the P.N.E. officials was in the latter part of February and they assured us that they had dropped all plans for ice facilities in the new building and that it would be devoted to the needs of the livestock industry.
What date was that?
The latter part of February.

Mr. Chairman, so much has been said about the building that I wonder whether the minister would allow the P.N.E. to have the money to construct a building anywhere in the city of Vancouver, not necessarily on the exhibition grounds? We all know, for example, that McGill university is in downtown Montreal but I have noticed on my way into the city that the part of the university having to do with farming is located to the west of Montreal. If money were given to McGill I imagine that some part of it would find its way into the operation west of Montreal. The same thing could apply in this instance. We could have our livestock show downtown if necessary and we would all be happy.

On the last day this matter came up I asked the Minister of Agriculture if he could enlighten us with respect to the definition of exhibition grounds and I said that I hoped he would be able to inform himself on the matter during the intervening time. So that the point may be straightened out so far as the people of Vancouver are concerned, I ask the minister specifically whether or not the acquisition of land in downtown Vancouver for exhibition purposes would mean that that land would be considered part of the exhibition grounds? I think there is a general principle involved which would apply to many other cities. Would the minister be good enough to comment?

The regulations for grants to exhibitions are under review and we took up the matter with the provincial ministers of agriculture at the agricultural ministers' conference. I should like to point out to hon. members that the grant to the Pacific national exhibition is completely outside the regulations. It is a special grant as a matter of grace and such grants go to very few exhibitions. It is being made in this case because the Pacific national exhibition has certain national characteristics. The only other exhibition that has qualified is the Royal at Toronto and I believe a similar grant has been proposed for another city. It is only when some national significance can be established that we give these special grants. So far as the location of buildings is concerned, all we are interested in is making sure that the purposes of agriculture are being advanced. We have no responsibility for athletics or public health.

Could we have a further statement from the minister that he will at least make an effort to discuss a larger grant with the Minister of Trade and Commerce? I am completely satisfied at the present time that an ice plant is going to be installed in the building. I am not concerned about what was said in letters. I am satisfied there are going to be ice facilities so if we are going to have hockey in the building why can we not have trade and commerce activities too?
Item agreed to.

Is the Postmaster General going to make a statement before we proceed with the items?
Supply-Post Office

Mr. Chairman, the greatest volume of postal business ever, the highest revenues in history, the most sweeping expansions in service to the public since 1867 and the boldest and most effective economy moves within the operational records of the department- this, in a nutshell, is the story of the postal service during the period between May 27, 1960, when I last presented the estimates of the Post Office Department for the consideration of the house, and the present.
During the last few years the volume of mail originating in Canada has spiralled upward in an apparently endless climb. When figures for this fiscal year are complete we will undoubtedly, for the first time in our history, top the four billion mark, or well over 200 pieces of mail for every man, woman and child in this country.
This staggering volume of mail is reflected in the department's revenues for the year
1960-61 which will top the $200 million mark for the first time in our history. When our figures are complete we expect to find we have incurred total expenditures in the neighbourhood of $209,500,000, thus showing a deficit on the year's operations of some $9 million. Since salary increases alone have cost us some $13J million during the year, I feel that our financial record remains most satisfactory. In the year just starting we will have the benefit of increased revenue from parcel post rate changes and our overall operations should therefore again be approximately on the break-even basis which it is my policy to try to maintain.
As a basis of comparison, Mr. Chairman, I might say that in the United States the post office department reported a net deficit of $597.1 million for the fiscal year 1960. Its annual report noted that $6.8 billion of the $15.3 billion increase in the national debt which has occurred since 1946 has been caused by postal deficits alone. I do not propose to deal in any more detail with overall finances since the general figures I have quoted are all that are yet available for the year ended March 31, 1961, and those for the preceding year are given in detail in our published report which is available to each member of the house.
During the year we have accomplished some remarkable economies in the face of marked cost increases that are above and beyond our control. One of the most remarkable of these has been in our Christmas mail operations where I am pleased to report the first major operational breakthrough in streamlined mail handling, a breakthrough that resulted in savings to the department in excess of $800,000.

Supply-Post Office
This tremendous saving has been accomplished in the face of a Christmas mail volume at least 5 per cent higher than that reported last year and despite the fact that no less than 10 new letter carrier offices have been added to the service in the past 12 months requiring a total of some 22,000 new Christmas man-hours in themselves.
In all, this year we cut our Christmas man-hours by some 115,000 over last year. These tremendous savings were accomplished by a combination of tight operational control and a simplified system of handling our Christmas card mail which we call terminal sortation.
Terminal sortation has gone hand in hand with a new system of separating first class mail from Christmas cards at the point where they first enter the mail stream. By a combination of these systems we have been able to provide service on regular mail during December that compares favourably with our standards for other months of the year. In short this past December we handled more mail, faster and at less cost than ever before in our history.
The steady increase in mail volume demands that we continue strenuous efforts to develop and perfect modern and effective mail handling techniques and equipment. One of our major projects in this field is the electronic-mechanical letter sortation system, the experimental model of which is being developed by the post office with the assistance of Canadair Limited in Montreal. We are at a crucial point in this development, for this ultra modern system has now reached the point of operational tests and is actually sorting regular mail for the Montreal post office.
Since this equipment is radically different from anything previously developed for postal purposes anywhere in the world, our present studies will provide the first practical figures for performance characteristics and output of such equipment. I can report that while the accuracy of the sorting system seems excellent, its reliability for continuing performance without mechanical or electronic failure is not as yet satisfactory and our tests indicate that some substantial additional work will be required on certain components.
Before proceeding with this project on any extended basis it is our intention to relate the information we have now obtained with certain other studies of a systems nature; based on the results we will decide the direction of our further advance.
There can be no doubt that during the past year we have made more progress than at any other time toward the ultimate production of an electronic-mechanical letter sortation

system. It is frustrating not to have shiny new batteries of such machines already installed in major Canadian post offices, but no other nation has reached this point because of the problems involved; and our system of advancing only as rapidly as we can be certain of the correctness of our advance undoubtedly gives the taxpayer far better value for every dollar spent than does any other method.
For example, our mailmobile system has proved its worth on a trial basis with only a limited number of machines, but the trials also demonstrated the need for a more rugged type of vehicle to meet the unusually difficult conditions of mail delivery. Sixteen machines manufactured by the builders of the famous "jeep" have been placed in service for test purposes along these lines.
Again, the experimental group of plastic letter boxes we tried out demonstrated that the material was completely satisfactory but that certain design changes were required and these are now being made before we proceed. In other words, we test and we determine what is right before we expend the taxpayers' money in large sums in fields where we are not absolutely certain of our position.
With respect to machinery and equipment of a highly advanced nature which is sufficiently proven to justify installation for regular use, we are engaged in a steady program of planning and development designed to improve the capacity of our existing buildings and to add new space to house such machinery. One such item will be a new chain type conveyor scheduled for the new wing of the Hamilton, Ontario post office which will permit mail bags and other loads to be moved at steep angles and guided and controlled by preset remote direction. The new building at Quebec and the new wing at Halifax will contain revolutionary new conveyor systems capable of lifting mail vertically on a continuous basis. They are the first such developments in this country and among the first on the continent. We will be installing at Winnipeg early next year a complex new mail segregator which will for the first time use electronic-mechanical techniques to perform automatically one of the most tiresome and time consuming chores presently performed by hand in post offices.
One tiny item that will nevertheless be of interest to anyone who has ever struggled and tried to write with post office pens is that we are trying a second experiment in the use of ball point pens in 14 of our major post offices. We also have ready for installation 300 of our electric stamp vending machines to which I referred last year and which

operate merely by dropping in the quarter without any further effort being required on the part of the patron. These machines will be in use shortly right across Canada in our post offices and other locations.
The handling of the mails within post offices is only part of the over-all job of communication which the post office must undertake. The other basic problem in postal services is transportation, and in this field we have made some of the most interesting and potentially important experiments of the year. One of the most intriguing has been our testing of "piggy-back" mail services which allow us to combine the best features of railway transportation and highway transportation in the swift movement of the mails. It is as yet too early to evaluate fully the results of these tests but it is apparent that the system offers some unique solutions to mail transport problems. Piggy-back services are designed primarily, of course, for the movement of second, third and fourth class mail, since the bulk of our first class letter mail travels by air.
As the number of trains available for the conveyance of mail continues to decline, the volume of mail handled by rail continues to increase, especially between the larger cities and on transcontinental services for whenever it has been possible to do so, we have continued to make use of the railways. In many cases we have made complicated adjustments in order to preserve a traditional railway link. A recent example is the change in service on trains five and six between Truro and Sydney, Nova Scotia. I think it is fair to say that without the determined co-operation of the post office in working out methods of handling mail on a difficult and more complex new schedule, the railway would have been forced to discontinue this line, and this action could have been a serious blow to the entire Cape Breton area.
We have, however, frequently been forced to accept alternative methods of transportation when existing rail links were terminated or reduced to the point where they no longer provided an acceptable service for the transportation of the mails. One such alternative is highway transport. In the last year we added no less than 53 new highway services, and made extensions in 46 existing routes. In addition, another eight routes have been approved and will be going into service shortly and five other routes are being seriously considered.
The final stage in the handling of mail is delivery to the patron. In rural areas during the past year 98 new rural routes have either been established or are authorized and will shortly go into service while 1,157 extensions have been made to existing routes.

It is also interesting to note that by this change we were able to provide approximately
5,000	additional firms with a second delivery, whereas previously they had received only one delivery each day. At the moment something closely approaching 100,000 business firms and locations are receiving two mail deliveries, or better, each day.

As our urban populations continue to increase we are faced with a new problem of providing adequate service to communities within communities, to the almost self-contained suburbs, many of which have populations as large or larger than some of our established cities.
One solution to this problem has been the increasing use of postal stations and letter carrier depots scattered at strategic points throughout the cities. During the last year we set in operation no less than 11 new postal stations and letter carrier depots which is, so far as we can judge, the greatest expansion in this type of service in the department's recent history. For the four-year period from 1957 to the present we opened more than twice as many of these stations as during the four-year period from 1953 to 1957.

This system is still in effect for those who wish it, but in addition, if a patron wishes, arrangements can be made by telephone for the item to be delivered on a specific day for a charge of 25 cents. Mr. Chairman, to come back to those mail-mobiles, the minister said in the house, in reply to a question of mine, that his department had purchased 57 mailmobiles at an average cost of $81,966 a year. Therefore, it would have been cheaper than the experiment he is now carrying out with those mail-mobiles.

I come now to that famous question of publicity. I know that our friend, the Postmaster General is publicity-minded. In fact, I have never known a minister to enjoy facing camera as much as does the present minister.
And yet in years gone by he would complain about the high cost of publicity, criticizing the publicity reports for 1956 and 1957.
Well in 1956-57, before the minister took over his present function, we used to spend $326,700 in Canada for his department's publicity. We are now asked in this budget to vote $456,800 for the same purpose, which is an increase of more than $130,000, or one third; that amount is more than sufficient to replace the famous locks the keys of which are now in the hands of Kingston inmates.
I believe that in that field alone he could save enough to change all locks on postal boxes which may be broken into, since it has been proven by the police who inquired into the matter that crooks had keys to open almost any postal box across the country.
As a proof of his propensity for exaggeration, the Postmaster General uses public money for his own publicity. I have here a copy of the publication entitled Postmark, for which the government spends over $34,000 every year.
If you get this little publication, you will notice that every issue carries a photograph of the Postmaster General. It is reproduced sometimes twice, sometimes three times. I have even found an issue showing his picture 12 times. Altogether, these publications printed the picture of our sweet Postmaster General 70 times.
In addition, he has been cover-boy or pinup boy seven or eight times. He has been photographed standing up, riding a scooter, a car, sorting mail and bowling. He has been photographed from the front and from the back.
In all this publicity we find summaries of things he has said, and references to the places where he has been and where he has eaten.
All that has cost the Canadian public $34,000. We have no objection to the minister making propaganda for himself, and I believe he needs it. He has my approval, but he should do it at his own expense, not at the expense of the Canadian people.
But that was not enough to satisfy him, so he recently sent another 24-page book, printed on de luxe paper. I got one and I believe other members got a copy too.
In this book, he tells us that we do not know anything about postal service. However, on reading the book, we realize that the Postmaster General himself does not know anything about it either.

His name appears on page one, and again on page three.
Another blank page and a nice grey ribbon.

The minister boasts of having set up carrier services. However this service has been refused to Ste. Agathe des Monts; and do you know why? They did not have the required population. Therefore, it was not the minister's fault. Well, same goes for those who have obtained their carrier service-it was not the minister's doing either. Carrier service extension is normal, as evidenced by the annual increases of those services.
In 1956-57, street letter box service increased by eight; in 1957-58, it increased by nine; there has been another increase in 1958-59 and an increase of nine in 1959-60.
As far as parcel post is concerned, it is the same thing; each year you add four or five new services-it is normal.
Therefore, the minister should not take credit for it. It depends on the population, the area and the density of homes.
The situation is the same in the case of the other road services.
In the case of rural routes, they used to increase by about 50 each year in the past. The minister does exactly the same thing now. The policy was the same in 1956-57 when those routes increased by 50; in 1959-60, they increased by 54. This is nothing to boast about. There is no reason to take any credit for it. Everything is done according to rules established long before the hon. gentleman became Postmaster General.
As far as the post offices are concerned, the minister cannot boast of having increased their number because, since he took over they have decreased by exactly 382. Some better and larger ones have been built but nevertheless, we have, in this country, 382 post offices less than when the minister's party took over.
A few moments ago, the efficiency of the service which looks after compensation claims was mentioned. In 1957, there were 11,800 claims; in 1959-60, there were 13,020. Consequently, since the minister has been administering the department, compensation claims have not decreased.
Compensation paid in 1957, because they were really warranted, amounted to $128,000, whereas under the present minister's administration, his department paid out a sum of $170,000 in compensation. In short, as far as an improvement of that service is concerned, it can scarcely be called a success.

I suggest that the hon. member bear with me for two or three minutes. In any event, he knows full well that we are allowed to speak for 30 minutes when the house is considering estimates, and to rise as often as we wish. I also think the Postmaster General is anxious to get rid of me as soon as possible, and I want to give him satisfaction.
I still have to deal with the matter of thefts, for which I should not need more than two minutes. The present minister used to complain that his predecessor hired thieves. He has risen to office, he has become Post-

master General, and now there are even more thefts. And when he was asked about this, he said: "Yes, there are more thefts, but there is less money involved." This year however, there are more thefts and there is more money involved. I wonder what excuse he will turn up. Let me remind him of what he said on July 26 1958, as recorded on page 2739 of Hansard:
.. .while roberries in post offices did increase from 159 in the previous year to 191, the actual losses in those robberies declined from $161,500 to $130,100. The reason for that is simply that instead of the previous, self-satisfied, take-what-may-come attitude of the former postmaster general we went after this thing.
The minister says he went after this thing. Could it be because there had been less money stolen? In 1959-1960 the number of thefts reached the figure of 813. At the time he complained, there had been 335. So what kind of success can the minister claim? The amount of money stolen at the time was $106,510, as against $295,130 today. In other words, the amount has tripled and the number of thefts has doubled. So, considering that he used to complain about the minister hiring thieves, I wonder what charge I should level at the present minister now.
Mr. Chairman, in order to please the hon. member who finds that my comments are not likely to help the Conservative party, I shall close my remarks in saying that the Postmaster General has fulfilled none of the numerous promises he made when he was a private member.
Second, he has neglected the employees in lowering their morale by his meanness.
Third, he has neglected the services in multiplying delays, in allowing thefts to increase, in allowing, for instance, that deliveries by truck be exposed to thefts much more than when deliveries were made by train. Allow me to remind the house that when one of the first postal services was set up in 1719, highway robbers had been checked by arming mail couriers. The minister could do the same thing; he could also investigate when a mail transport contract is granted. I submit that the present minister is not aware of the behaviour or background of those who obtain mail contracts, nor of the truck drivers. No wonder the mail is exposed to all kinds of thefts, as was the case when the truck driver was himself the thief. I suggest to the minister to reconsider the matter and stop increasing truck transport to the detriment of railway transport.

Lately, we learned that the Canadian National Railways had registered a deficit of $67 million. That would be a good opportunity to reduce that deficit a little by having them keep their contracts.
Once again, I hope the minister will give credit to those postal employees who are doing a tremendous job, and who certainly deserve the congratulations of the Canadian people.

Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, some 10 minutes ago the hon. member who has the floor said that he would finish in two or three minutes. These have been the longest two or three minutes that I have ever experienced in my life.

Mr. Chairman, some of us have looked forward with anticipation to once again having our annual entertainment in the House of Commons and I must say that the hon. member for St. Denis has not let us down. He has again provided enjoyment in our discussions. I should like to disagree with him on only one plea that he appeared to be making. If I assess his submissions accurately, he seemed to plead with the department to delay the application of automation to the Post Office Department in the interest of supplying more employment in our nation. To me this would be a most deplorable attitude for the minister or for any department of government or any industry to adopt because I believe that all of us ought to basically welcome the advance of automation. If we can make machines do the work that human labour has done in the past I believe it is in the long term interest of all of us to welcome this type of development. I believe that national unemployment problems have to be resolved in another way and that opposing automation in any department of government or in any industry is a very poor answer to the unemployment problem.
In my initial remarks I should like to remind the minister of the call issued by his own Prime Minister at the last meeting of the national Progressive Conservative party of Canada in their great pow-wow in Ottawa, at which time the Prime Minister announced that the issue the next time we faced the electorate will be free enterprise versus socialism. Since the minister is one of those responsible for the operation of one of the most socialistic enterprises in our nation, I ask him whether tenders have yet been called for the sale of the Post Office Department? Is he prepared to follow his leader and offer for public sale the enterprise known as the 90205-6-231
Supply-Post Office
post office of Canada because, if I understand the clarion call of the next election, it is supposed to be free enterprise versus socialism. The minister is responsible for one of the greatest socialistic enterprises in Canada, and I am asking him whether the post office is to be sold to private enterprise with or without tenders being asked for and bids being called?
I should also like to join the hon. member for St. Denis in his expression of regret over the "letter perfect" that we received in our mails. I should like especially to express my regret at the particular bulletin entitled the "Letter Perfect." We received a letter signed by William Hamilton, Postmaster General. I suppose it was signed by a mimeograph machine. What I do not particularly appreciate is the opening sentence which asks, "How much do you know about the Canadian post office? If you are like most other Canadians the answer is 'very little' ". I think the tone of that letter is regrettable in so far as the recipients are concerned. I know the minister is an expert in the field of public relations and advertising. However, I am sure that no one in the advertising field, or in the public relations field, will agree with him that it was appropriate to address that letter to all members of parliament, and I suppose to all members of the other place, informing them that what they know about the Canadian post office is "very little".
I believe this was a regrettable move on the part of the Post Office Department and it did very little to enhance the prestige of the minister. We may all be experts in certain fields but if we have an understanding of public relations we will never inform people that they are not also experts in a particular field.
I should like to begin my remarks by paying my compliments to the employees of the minister's department. I believe that in world history instances are very rare where public employees can be said to have given as faithful service to the general public as have the employees of the Canadian post office over many long years. They have done so despite inadequate wages and inadequate recognition on the part of the government of Canada in years gone by.
To come to specific matters. I recall that some time ago the minister assured the house that the minimum number of households required before door-to-door delivery service might be instituted in any community was a subject that was under consideration. At the present time the regulations provide that door-to-door delivery service cannot be instituted in any community until at least 2,500 households exist. The minister assured the house at that time that this minimum figure was under active consideration from the point of view

Supply-Post Office
of the possibility of reducing it. I should like to have a report as to what have been the results of this active consideration. Have any conclusions been reached and, if so, what are the conclusions?
In the light of existing levels of unemployment I believe very serious consideration indeed should be given to this matter and I should like to recommend that door-to-door delivery be instituted in all communities having 1,500 households rather than the existing minimum of 2,500. Before we go overboard in offering twice-daily service in any of our urban areas for the convenience of a limited number of business institutions, I believe we should first of all give most serious consideration to reducing the minimum number of households required before an urban area, a suburban area or any postal community can have door-to-door delivery service.
I should like to call the minister's attention to page 48 of his latest annual report. I notice that it deals with the year ended March 31, 1960. I suppose that a day or two after we have completed his estimates we will receive in the mail the latest annual report for the year ended March 31, 1961.
Thank you for the compliment.

I have noticed this happening in the case of so many departments in the past. The moment the estimates are through we are supplied with a copy of the latest annual report. I can understand that as of today, April 13, the minister can hardly be expected to have his annual report completed and I am willing to forgive him. However, I regret having to deal with a report that is over a year old.
I should like to call his attention to page 48 where reference is made to the operations of the post office savings bank for the past ten fiscal years. In my opinion this is a wonderful institution and I regret that the minister and his department are doing very little indeed to advertise the facilities available to the Canadian public through the branches of the post office savings bank that exist.
I am very pleased to note that the number of depositors has increased. There are now 302,611 accounts compared with 278,595 at March 31, 1951. I believe that is remarkable progress. However, I also notice that the balance on deposit as at the end of the fiscal year has declined from $37,661,920.55 at March 31, 1951, to $29,372,460.93 as of March 31, 1960. In my view this is regrettable. I contend that the minister and the Post Office Department should undertake measures to make the facilities available to the Canadian

public more widely known. I look forward to the number of depositors who patronize the post office savings bank continuing to grow and I hope the total volume of deposits will also grow in the years to come.
I should now like to refer the minister to page 50 of his latest annual report where reference is made to the number of post offices. Once again, as I have done in other years, I must call his attention to the fact that there is again a decline in the number of post offices in operation in Canada. During the year ended March 31, 1960, there were 279 post offices closed while only 142 new post offices were established resulting in a net decline in the number of post offices of 137. The reason I raise this issue is that it is a very important one to many people living in the suburban areas adjacent to the metropolitan centres of Canada. There is and there has been for years a deliberate policy on the part of the Post Office Department to lock up post offices in suburban communities in order to enhance the prestige and size of the major post office in the central metropolitan area. The minister should realize that he is not being blamed for the Liberals having built a $14 million lemon in Vancouver. He ought not to sustain the maintenance of that lemon and to penalize all rural communities around Vancouver for the sake of making this Vancouver lemon into a paying proposition. The minister ought to realize that there was a minister preceding him and that there were other colleagues of the minister preceding him who looked with envy at the pork barrels existing in Montreal and in Toronto and who made a very desperate effort to establish a similar pork barrel in the city of Vancouver. We are having post offices closed down and knocked out of business all around Vancouver, even many miles away from Vancouver, because of this initial plot and scheme for which I do not blame the minister. It was a Liberal cabinet minister, and not even a former Liberal postmaster general but a Liberal cabinet minister of the city of Vancouver, who designed this particular plot.
If the minister attempts to tell me or the people of the lower mainland that because of automation efficiency is being increased, he is completely wrong. He can ask any reputable business man in the lower mainland of British Columbia and he will find that our services are deteriorating year by year until the situation has arrived at the stage where every once in a while delivery of a first class letter from Ottawa to my home takes up to five days, while a letter out of South Burnaby into north Burnaby will take up to three and four days. Any man, on behalf of a business enterprise or organization sending out mail

in the lower mainland of British Columbia will be very happy to substantiate my claim. The minister is not responsible initially. He ought to stop listening to the big grass in the Vancouver postal district and pay some attention to the local community needs in that area. Our postal services are rapidly deteriorating.
We see no beneficial results whatsoever in this effort to build up this horrible lemon we find on Georgia Street which cost the taxpayers $14 million. A tunnel was built, if you please, to carry the mail from the C.P.R. station. It is an underground tunnel. I do not know how long it is; it is several miles in length and it cost $2 million. It has been a complete flop ever since the beginning. All important mail goes by air as the minister knows. The building was designed for helicopter service from the airport to the post office. I understand there is no such service even yet after many long years. There is no helicopter that takes the mail at the airport and delivers it on to the roof of this $14 million building. However, to handle the advertising of the soapsuds there is a $2 million tunnel in operation.
I would ask the minister whether the interest on $2 million a year would not more than pay for all the trucking necessary for a number of years to come. There is no tunnel to the C.N.R. station. There is just one tunnel costing $2 million to the C.P.R. station. I understand that it is operating most inefficiently and that, as far as economics are concerned, it is really something fantastic and out of this world.
I hope the post office will also soon begin to pay some attention to municipal boundaries. I know the assertion is made that in the interests of efficiency they can pay no attention to municipal boundaries. However, I have in my constituency the corporation of the district of Coquitlam. The residents of this municipality receive their mail either in the city of Coquitlam, out at the city of New Westminster or out at the city of Port Moody -and that is a fantastic situation-simply because of the arbitrary authority. We pay no attention to municipal boundaries. It is ridiculous. If there were a little bit of good will on the part of the postal authorities, they would pay some attention at least to municipal borders and would attempt to align their services so as to cause the least possible disruption. In my opinion it is completely needless that one single municipality must be served out of three separate post offices, each with a different name.

mail. I feel that it is absolutely unfair to ask the users of first class mail and the taxpayers of Canada to subsidize all the horrible material that arrives in our mail boxes almost every day.
