The taxpayers and the users of first class mail are helping to pay for the distribution of this kind of junk. These companies, if you please, can turn around and claim this cost under the Income Tax Act as part of their advertising expenses. I know what happens to this 12 cents. Every merchant in Ottawa has 100 customers who like their merchant and they do not buy the stuff. They just bring the coupons to the merchants. It means in this case roughly 49 cents to these merchants to whom these advertisement coupons will be delivered in time.
I believe it is time that these misusers of the Canadian postal facilities are made to pay their fair share of the cost. This has nothing to do with the distribution of public information as is the case when we speak of newspapers or other valuable publications. However, these people ought to be called to account and be made to pay their fair share.
I should also like to ask the minister about one other matter. How much does his department pay each year to Pitney-Bowes? How much did they pay within the last fiscal year, or the fiscal year preceding that, if that information happens to be statistically more easily available to the minister?
If I want a Pitney-Bowes machine, why do I have to pay much more than the little machine is worth in the first place in order to get it to my business office? Then why

Supply-Post Office
do I have to pay a rental every three months on the machine? In the average business establishment the rental alone is more than the bloomin' little machine is worth in the first place.
I ask the minister, does Pitney-Bowes have a complete monopoly in the matter of postage meters; and if so, why? Why does not the department consider owning its own machines and renting them out to business establishments in Canada? Why do we have to pay over $300 for a machine that in its manufacture is worth perhaps $8 or $9, and then have to pay a very heavy rental ever after? What kind of a stranglehold have these people on the post office in this regard?
While I know they have not a monopoly in this field, how much did the government pay Pitney-Bowes in the last recorded year for the rental of weighing scales; and if they rent any at all, have they paid any money to Pitney-Bowes for the rental of folding machines? My inquiry concerns postage meters, scales and folding machines.
I believe the activities of this particular firm in relationship to the post office are due for investigation and I should like to have the minister's observations on these matters.
Before resuming my seat my main plea to the minister is that he should realize that in 1957 he became the Postmaster General of Canada. I know that most of his employees are loyal beyond the call of duty. However, I should not like the minister to think for one moment that he must always and at all times heed the advice of his senior officials without personal investigation into the merits of the arguments put forward by those senior officials.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to congratulate the Postmaster General on a very interesting presentation of the annual report of his department. The hon. member for St. Denis could not see too much virtue in it, but I think the hon. member is possibly better as a humourist than a statesman, as far as his view of post office matters is concerned.
I think the Post Office Department, the Postmaster General and the government are to be congratulated for taking a forward view in carrying on the administration of this branch of government service. No service given to the Canadian people is nearer to their hearts, lives or emotions than the service given by the Post Office Department.
Steps were taken during the last year to promote good relations with the employees of this department by adjusting their wages and bringing them into line with other adjustments that have been made throughout the civil service. I am sure that the morale

of post office employees has been greatly improved over the year on that account.
I know the Postmaster General is well liked by his employees. He has come into my own constituency without any fanfare and has visited local post offices in a quiet and efficient way much to the liking of the people in charge of those post offices. The department has been alert to increase the delivery service in the urban development areas around the city of London, and this has been much appreciated.
On behalf of the people of my constituency I extend thanks to the Postmaster General and the government for the promise of some new post office construction in our riding in the towns of Strathroy, Lucan and the village of Delaware.
I should like to offer one suggestion to the minister and the government for the improvement of the post office service in Canada. I suggest that the government give consideration to extending house-to-house delivery to the smaller centres. At the present time we have house-to-house delivery in the cities and, as was pointed out in the report of the Postmaster General, in the business sections there are two deliveries a day in many instances.
In the well developed rural areas all across the country we have house-to-house delivery through the medium of rural delivery carriers. In the smaller towns and villages across the country people still have to walk a distance of up to half a mile to the post office for their mail. I think it would be worth considering extending house-to-house delivery in the smaller towns and villages where this can be done with reasonable facility.
We are spending large sums of money to encourage the creation of jobs in Canada. Here would be a field of employment really made to measure. It requires only manpower.
It has been estimated by some authorities that in the heavy construction industry it costs as much as $28,000 a year to keep one man working with modern equipment. This is because of the high capital cost of materials and the power equipment necessary for this kind of industry. It would cost virtually nothing in the way of capital to put a mail carrier to work. Every dollar spent would be a dollar in wages. Such a program would constitute the most direct possible form of encouraging employment.
Such an extension of house-to-house delivery would raise our standard of living and assist in the equitable sharing of our national income by supplying more people with gainful employment. On January 22, 1959 I made the same suggestion in the

course of the debate on the address and I said on that occasion as reported on page 225 of Hansard:
On page 2744 of Hansard of July 26, 1958 the Postmaster General (Mr. Hamilton) stated that house-to-house delivery is not provided in municipalities where delivery calls number less than 2,500. The reason behind this policy is that house-to-house delivery is most economical where six carriers can be used, five for regular five-day week route work and one spare man to alternate over the five regular routes so as to furnish six-day service.
It is respectfully suggested to the minister and the government that consideration should now be given to providing house-to-house delivery in smaller towns and villages where there is sufficient work to provide full-time employment for one man. Rural free delivery is almost universal; so is house-to-house delivery in the large centres. It would appear that the people in the smaller towns and villages may be under a disadvantage compared with others from the standpoint of mail service.
I should like to suggest to the Postmaster General and to the government that an estimate of the cost of extending house-to-house delivery to the smaller towns and villages across Canada be made, and that careful consideration should be given to the proposal I have outlined.

Like all hon. members I listened with a great deal of interest to what the minister had to tell us about his department this afternoon. I want to compliment him on the achievements which he related to the committee, although the evident satisfaction which the minister showed in those achievements might perhaps make any further compliments seem superfluous.
Before proceeding, I too, want to pay tribute to the staff of the post office both here in Ottawa and in my own province. As the Postmaster General has said, they are very dedicated people and I wish to record my appreciation of the co-operation I have always received from them and for the thoughtful and sympathetic consideration which they have always given to problems I have brought before them.
Like the hon. member for St. Denis I received one of those little booklets telling the story of the Canadian postal service, and I want to thank the Postmaster General for reminding me that I am both a shareholder and a patron of our country's most essential public service utility. As a shareholder in this great public service over which the Postmaster General presides I must confess that my chest swelled with pride at the great list of broken records and earth shattering achievements about which the hon. gentleman told us this afternoon but I must say also that this pride was rudely dissipated when the Postmaster General announced a $9 million deficit. Deficits are always bad news to
Supply-Post Office
shareholders and it came as an anti-climax to all those great accomplishments:	the
greatest volume, the greatest expansion, the greatest revenue, he said, since 1867. The minister did not say it, but I was wondering whether this deficit was also the greatest deficit we have had since 1867.
No.

Well, I did note from the report that this is the greatest deficit we have had since 1951. The largest deficit recorded since 1951 is a little under $2| million. We had a surplus in 1956 amounting, I think, to a little more than $10 million, which is a far cry from the financial balance sheet which the minister put on record today. The Postmaster General explained that this deficit was due to salary increases. I do not think that explanation is entirely valid. As the hon. member for St. Denis has pointed out there was an increase in the estimate last year as well as an increase in revenue, which should have helped toward paying those salary increases. The question which is uppermost in my mind is this: did any of those salary increases go to revenue postmasters? The minister mentioned two groups and I understood that these were permanent employees. But in most of my riding we have very small communities and very small post offices and I should think the people who work in them are not regarded as permanent employees but, more or less, as casual employees. I was wondering whether they also had shared in these increases. The minister nods; I am glad to know that they did.
In my province, or, at least, in my own riding, the functions of the post office have changed considerably over the past 12 or 13 years. Prior to confederation, or what we call confederation, when Newfoundland became a part of Canada, there were very few if any people in the ordinary fishing settlement who had any interest in the post office. The local merchant would probably be expecting mail together with the teacher, the clergyman and a few professional people. But perhaps not more than a dozen people in the whole settlement would be interested in the post office and therefore there was not too much concern about the service on the part of the people generally. Nowadays, however, everybody is interested in the post office because everybody gets mail. There are unemployment insurance cheques, family allowance cheques, old age pension cheques and so on, and the post office today instead of serving perhaps a dozen people serves practically every family in the community.
This places a greater burden on post office services and gives greater status to the postmaster. In view of this increase in traffic

Supply-Post Office
the postal accommodation situation in the small settlements is not satisfactory. We have a great number of settlements comprising 500 or 600 to 1,000 people. Although these settlements have quite a number of inhabitants the post office, because of low revenue, is operated from an individual's home. I am speaking of those settlements where the postal revenue is not great enough to warrant the provision of a post office building in the community. This situation imposes an inconvenience upon the residents because they must line up outdoors in all kinds of weather in order to receive their mail. Generally speaking there is no lobby in the private home and sometimes hardly even room enough to accommodate the mail.
I have repeatedly asked the Postmaster General to change the policy in this regard because I feel that if we are making great progress, as he has suggested this afternoon, the policy should surely be sufficiently flexible as to meet the varying conditions that exist in these settlements. I feel that we are, instead of changing the policy, holding to the old rigid policy of not providing postal services, such as buildings, etc., in those areas unless the revenue is at least $10,000, or something in that neighbourhood. This policy does not allow the provision of that type of service expected by the people in those out of the way settlements. I would like at this time to renew my age-old plea to the Postmaster General to reconsider his policy in this regard, and I hope that when he comes back to present his estimates next year he will be in a position to tell us that another great step forward has been taken in respect of a change in the provision of accommodation in the settlements to which I have been referring.
That would mean a greater deficit.

No, I do not think this would mean a greater deficit at all.
I would also like to bring a problem to the attention of the Postmaster General regarding the basis of remuneration to the postmasters in these small revenue areas, and suggest that it is not entirely fair. As the Postmaster General appreciates, the postmasters in these revenue areas are paid a fixed amount out of which they are required to provide accommodation, fuel, light, janitorial services and maintenance. This is a satisfactory system in some areas but does not work out well in others. One result of this policy is that in two areas, comparable both in size and work load, the cost of accommodation varies, with the result that one postmaster will, in effect, receive less than an other. I realize that there is the one advantage

that the total amount paid to individual postmasters can be used as a basis for superannuation, but it seems to me it would be more equitable if the Postmaster General were to accept the responsibility of providing for accommodation rather than placing the burden upon the individual postmasters themselves. Present practice does constitute a hardship to the individual postmasters in many cases. While it is true that, as the Postmaster General told us this afternoon, the salaries to revenue postmasters have been increased, I am wondering if there has been a proportionate increase given to cover the cost of rentals, fuel and other operating expenses, or is the increase in these costs to be taken care of by the one increase he mentioned?
I must now turn to a consideration as a patron rather than a shareholder and in this light must express concern at the increasing postal rates particularly in respect of parcel post services. As the hon. member for St. Denis pointed out, the rate increases have been substantial, ranging from 100 per cent to 300 per cent.

You
must remember that the rates have gone downward as well.

Yes, they have gone downward as well but in so far as they have gone up it constitutes an extra tax. I have no quarrel with the theory that the post office should pay its own way and I think that is a very sound principle, but in view of the increase in volume that has taken place and considering the modernization that has been effected by the automatic mail handlers, surely there is a decrease in the unit handling cost which would offset any additional expenditures which the Post Office Department may have to make. I believe every large private organization operates on this theory and I feel that the Post Office Department should do the same.
In any case, if we consider last year's report of the Postmaster General we find that over a 10-year period there is a $30 million credit to the taxpayers in respect of postal services. I arrive at this figure by adding the surpluses of 1951 to 1960 inclusive, which total $34,765 million, and subtracting the deficit for the same period which amounted to $4,374 million. I think the taxpayer should be entitled to have this surplus taken into account when considering any increase in postal rates, particularly since increased efficiency of operation would perhaps offset any increase in operating expenditures.

The Postmaster General referred this afternoon to an honourable mention which had been given to a design for a special issue of postage stamps.
was referring to a first prize rather than an honourable mention.

Yes, I should have referred to the first prize and, for my purposes, that is even better. In this connection I am reminded of a letter I received some time ago from a Newfoundland organization which urged that a special stamp be issued at Christmas time depicting, perhaps, the scene of the nativity. I am not aware that the Postmaster General has received a similar letter but it originated with an organization that has dedicated itself to offsetting the commercialization of Christmas. It was pointed out in this letter that seven or eight other countries had issued several stamps in this vein at Christmas. I feel this is a good idea and would support this organization's request, and hope that the Postmaster General will give it favourable consideration.
In looking at the Postmaster General's report for last year I see that his department's greatest source of revenue is derived from the sale of postage stamps. I also notice that revenue from the sale of meters and registration impressions has almost equalled that from the sale of stamps. We have not been given the figures in this regard for the present year and do not know therefore if the increase in revenue from postal meters and registration impressions has taken place on the same scale, but if it has been proportionate then it is now perhaps even greater than the revenue from postage stamps.
Which of these two methods of selling stamps produces the greater net revenue for the post office? I understand that the only expense in connection with the stamps is the printing of the stamps themselves, which should not be too expensive. Is the cost of the meters greater than the cost of the postage stamps? If we are short of revenue, or are running into deficits, then we should encourage the method which will produce the greatest amount of net revenue.
The minister took a great deal of pride in the reduced number of complaints that he has received. Of course, there are two ways of looking at this. People sometimes give up complaining when they feel it is no use to complain. While they may have complained more when the Liberals were in power it may have been because they had more hope of getting action on their complaints. Now they have learned from experience that it is useless to complain to the Tories and they have given up in despair.
Supply-Post Office
Therefore, I would not advise the Postmaster General to press that argument too far.
There is just one other question I wish to ask the minister before I take my seat. I notice on the sheet entitled "Standard Objects and Expenses", under "Special categories", the allocation for this year is up by $2.8 million. The explanation indicates that the reason for this increase was the movement of mail by land, air and water. I was wondering whether the minister would tell us if this is on account of an increased volume of mail or on account of the increased cost of contracts that have been renewed? These are all the things I wish to mention at this time. There may be other points that I shall raise when we come to the individual items.

Mr. Chairman, as a former postmaster for almost 36 years, I am always interested in the estimates of the Post Office Department and especially in the wonderful growth of this organization and the splendid service provided by the Postmaster General, his department and thousands of employees across Canada.
Since retiring as a postmaster over three years ago I have been impressed by the many changes that have been made in the improvement of mail service during that short period.
The booklet entitled "Letter Perfect", about which we have heard quite a bit, the story of the Canadian postal service, published by authority of our Postmaster General, should be of great interest to all Canadians as shareholders and patrons of the Canada post office. The Postmaster General's remarks in the second paragraph of the foreword in this booklet are well worth repeating. I quote:
Keeping pace with the tremendous growth and development that have marked Canadian business and industry In recent years, the post office has worked hard to maintain a modern efficient organization that handles an ever-increasing amount of business with speed and economy.
The efforts of 40,000 or more employees at more than 11,000 post offices across Canada present to us some idea of the great volume of mail handled so efficiently. Transportation of mail, as we know, is provided by air, water, rail, motor vehicle, snowmobile, dog sled and by other means. Perhaps one of the finest improvements has been the regular letter mail by air, otherwise known as "all-up service". To give the committee an example of the value and speed of such service, a letter mailed at my former office in Elmira, Ontario, on Monday evening at six o'clock was received and ready for delivery in Halifax at 9.00 a.m. the next morning.

Supply-Post Office
Great strides have been made in the rural mail carrier service. This has given an additional number of Canadians the opportunity to enjoy this privilege for the first time. Owing to the increase in volume of mail, we realize that these carriers are spending more time in preparing the mail for delivery and longer hours in covering their routes. Most of these carriers have been compensated for this extra time, but others have not received any increases for some time. Owing to the higher cost of living, may I suggest to the director of transportation, who has made a noticeable contribution to the improvement of rural routes and other services under his direction, that he give this matter his further consideration.
Many other advancements have been ably explained by our Postmaster General in his opening remarks. The indications are that the Post Office Department is ever ready and always on the alert to improve such services for the benefit of all concerned.
The Post Office Department has often been referred to as the barometer of business. During my term of office in this department men of business, industry, labour and agriculture inquired from time to time as to the increases of revenue in order to analyse the development of Canada's economy as a whole. The Post Office Department, along with the district director and his staff, have always been very helpful and considerate in providing advice and information concerning post office problems and opportunities to better the service.
The appointment of area superintendents, according to my observation, has been invaluable to post offices in their areas, especially the smaller ones spread out in those districts. Their frequent visits give them the opportunity of personal contact with the postmaster and his staff and also to correct certain details so essential to the betterment of the postal service. In my opinion they are performing yeoman work.
The appointment of public relations officers has always been commendable. The public relations officer has played a large part in the courteous behaviour of the post office staff to Mr. John Public and vice versa. On various occasions this officer from the district director's department visited my office, at which time he called on the schools, spoke to the service clubs and showed pictures of the advancement of postal service; he explained in detail other important matters such as insurance, c.o.d., special delivery and the benefits of householder mail.
The explanation of the postal service to our younger folks has been carried out for some time. During the spring and fall seasons I would arrange with the principal and

teachers of our schools to have the children visit my office in their classes, at which time explanations concerning the service were given.
Perhaps I could mention at this time that the visits of our Postmaster General have been deeply appreciated. It gives the employees the feeling that they are important cogs in this great work.
May I express my appreciation to the Postmaster General and the Minister of Public Works of their interest and concern in postal facilities at Kitchener, Ontario. This city has doubled its population in the last 25 years, and the improvements in the facilities in our area have been beneficial to all concerned.
Kitchener's twin city, Waterloo, where the present post office was built in 1912 and improved in 1948, has doubled its population in the last 10 years and tripled its revenue during that time. Again may I say I appreciate the efforts that are being made to overcome the present inadequate accommodation.
The Ontario postmasters' association, along with other such groups throughout Canada, have been interested in the postmasters and their staffs who work in the smaller offices. I am sure that the Postmaster General, along with all employees, was saddened last year by the sudden passing of Mr. Jay Ferris, postmaster of Campbellford, Ontario. This gentleman held many important positions in the postmasters' association and along with others played a big part in the substantial increases recently received by employees and in other matters pertaining to the welfare of public servants.
As a former member of this association for many years and a supervisory postmaster, I can understand some of the problems facing the postmasters of smaller offices. Many of these people are unable to enjoy more than a few days holidays each year as their services are requested from day to day. May I suggest that special instructions could be given by the postmaster and the department to the postmaster's assistant covering all phases of the work, including the cash account.
I have noticed from time to time the announcements as to how mechanized the post office is becoming and the amount of research that is being done to improve mechanization. Perhaps most of this research is being directed toward the larger offices. This research could also be directed toward the smaller offices as no doubt they would welcome the introduction of small cancelling machines and adding machines in order to provide them with some kind of efficient tools in their trade. Without these machines they must continue to do everything manually.

Their manual labour in this regard and their other duties involving the savings bank, government annuities, distribution of income tax forms, unemployment insurance stamps, et cetera, provide a busy schedule for the postmaster and staff. May I recommend to the department that further consideration be given to the smaller offices with regard to such matters.
Another interesting point that has been discussed on many occasions and which was mentioned by the hon. member for Middlesex West is that patrons in smaller towns find it difficult to understand why they cannot obtain house-to-house delivery of their mail. They feel that the postage they pay is the same as people pay in the cities and that they should be entitled to the same consideration. However, I understand that the Post Office Department has certain minimum requirements that must be met. Perhaps these requirements may be set too high. Older people have to walk quite a distance to receive their mail and parcels while others in the cities have them delivered. After all, the same taxes are paid by the people in the smaller towns. I hope this problem can be reviewed.
My last point has reference to the possible application of the minimum, four-cent local or drop letter rate of postage between Kitchener and Waterloo. I know that the rates on letters are governed by the Post Office Act which stipulates that the rate of postage on each letter posted within one postal area for delivery in another postal area is five cents for the first ounce, et cetera. I know that at the present time Kitchener and Waterloo are classed as two separate and distinct postal areas. I wish to mention that, geographically speaking, you walk from one city to the other without noticing the difference. In fact, they are so close that some people's homes are half in Waterloo and half in Kitchener and they pay taxes to each city. At one time the mayor of Kitchener lived in Waterloo and the mayor of Waterloo lived in Kitchener. Many Kitchener people work in Waterloo and vice versa. Girls working in office positions often take the mail with them at closing time and drop such letters in their home post office with the result that they are marked "postage due", which causes dissatisfaction to the receiver. I understand that this problem is being studied further by the department.
It has been a privilege, Mr. Chairman, for me to take part in the discussion of these estimates. May I again commend the Postmaster General, his genial deputy and all the employees for the success they have achieved in this important department.

Mr. Chairman, the speech made by the Postmaster General was such a really marvellous job of polishing his own flawless
Business of the House
diamond that I hate to get up and put any mist on the jewel but I feel that the department is hardly as perfect as the Postmaster General perhaps is. I wish to make a number of comments about the organization of the department and particularly about its deficit.
The minister really did not really speak about the deficit, the amount of money the department is losing on certain parts of its operations, specifically in its handling of parcel post and second class mail, though he did make some reference to parcel post. It seems to me that with that business efficiency he brought to giving us this wonderful pamphlet, "Letter Perfect", with the taste for design he has brought to postage stamps and to letter boxes and the efficiency he has brought to expansions of services he should be able to do something a bit more positive than he has with regard to the deficit.
Another thing he failed to speak about is a subject he brought up in a speech he made when he was in the United States, a speech that I am sure he was delighted to see find a place in that very well known publication, "Vital Speeches of Today". This is not something that happens every day to a Canadian Postmaster General so one would have imagined he would be proud of the remarks he made there and the policy that he seemed to enunciate. I can only be somewhat aghast that he did not bother to work that subject into his speech tonight in leading off on his departmental estimates. Perhaps I can call it ten o'clock and get under way more properly tomorrow on my appreciation of the Postmaster General.
Resolutions adopted in committee of supply this day reported and concurred in.

Mr. Speaker, would the house leader indicate what the business may be for next week? I am assuming, of course, that we will continue with the estimates of the Post Office Department tomorrow followed, as he said last night, by the estimates of the Department of Fisheries. Are we to have a supply motion on Monday in view of the fact that the supply motion this week was postponed or is there other business for next week?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Friday's business will be as the hon. member has mentioned. We will continue with the estimates of the Post Office Department and if they are completed we will go on with the estimates of the Department of Fisheries.
The forecast for next week, subject to change because of changing circumstances as seems to happen almost every week, will be as follows: On Monday instead of a supply

Business of the House
motion we will take legislation. We will commence with item No. 3 on today's order paper, Bill No. C-72, an act to amend the Customs Tariff. That will be followed by Bill No. C-82, item No. 5 on today's order paper, having to do with a convention between Canada and the United States with regard to taxation matters. That will be followed by item No. 9 on today's order paper, the resolution in the name of the Minister of Labour dealing with the subject of rehabilitation of disabled persons. The estimates for next week, discussion of which may commence on Wednesday, will
be those of the Post Office Department if, unfortunately, we do not finish them tomorrow although I am sure the house will want to complete that department. We will then go on with the estimates of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. I think that is all I will announce by way of a forecast for next week. Perhaps I could enlarge on Monday evening if the house appears to have made good progress.
At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
The following answers, deposited with the Clerk of the house, are printed in the official report of debates pursuant to standing order 39:

1.	Does the Royal Canadian Air Force conduct aerial photography for the purpose of mapping and charting (a) in the Canadian Arctic (b) in any other area of Canada?
2.	If so, are the photographs developed as the result of these flights available for: (a) inspection and future use connected with the economic development of Canada (b) photogrammetry (c) photo interpretation (d) resources surveys (e) structural geology (f) forest inventory (g) overburden and soil analyses (h) land use surveys (i) airborne profile recording (j) photographic reproduction?
3.	If not, for what reason?
4.	Have all these photographs been kept under the best possible conditions for future use?
5.	Have there been any complaints from users of these photographs concerning their present quality because of deterioration due to improper storage?
Answer by: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister
of National Defence):

2 and 3. Prints of federal government negatives are available at a nominal charge to federal, provincial or civic governments, industry or the general public through the national air photo library of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys.
4.	Yes.
5.	No.
